title: R binds Snowflake semantic view variables without their declared type
description:
R can't call a Snowflake semantic view that declares a variable, at least with Snowflake ODBC driver 4.x. [`snowflake_semantic_metric_sql()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-r/R/catalog-snowflake.R#L763-L813) writes `VARIABLES "MIN_TOTAL" => ?` and binds the value. The driver binds it as text, and Snowflake requires a variable's value to match the declared type: `Expression's derived type 'VARCHAR(1)' does not match provided data type 'NUMBER(10,2)' for variable 'MIN_TOTAL'`.

`CAST(? AS NUMBER(10,2))` works. Casting to the type the view declares keeps the value exact. A looser cast such as `CAST(? AS NUMBER)` rounds `50.5` to `51`.

Found by "live Snowflake binds native semantic variables" in #431. That run used driver 4.0.0 on macOS. CI on Linux uses a different driver install, so it may not fail there, but the cast is correct with either driver.

title: R keeps the quotes in a Snowflake semantic view's quoted base table names
description:
R can't find the base tables of a Snowflake semantic view when the view names them with quoted identifiers. Snowflake stores the name exactly as written, so a base table created as `"orders"` appears in the view's YAML as `table: '"orders"'`. [`snowflake_semantic_dependencies()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-r/R/catalog-snowflake.R#L677-L707) keeps the quotes as part of the name. `data_source(con, tables = model$dependencies)` then fails with `tables names table not on the connection: "COMMONS_CI.LIVE.\"orders\""`.

The YAML follows SQL identifier rules: a quoted name is exact (with `""` for a literal quote), and an unquoted name folds to upper case. The same applies to `database` and `schema`.

Found by "live Snowflake scopes models associated with physical tables" in #431, the first live run with a semantic view provisioned.

title: Adding NULL to a date fails on Snowflake
description:
A definition that adds `NULL` to a date fails on Snowflake. `created + NULL` compiles to `"created" + NULL`, and Snowflake rejects it: `Invalid argument types for function '+': (DATE, NULL)`.

The type checker reads the expression as a temporal shift, because an untyped `NULL` is accepted as the interval, and gives it the type `datetime`. The emitters rewrite a temporal shift only when an operand has the type `interval`, so this one falls through to a plain `+`. Both packages have the same fault: [`_temporal_shift()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-py/src/commons/_definitions/_emit_sql.py#L415-L441) and [`definition_sql_temporal_shift()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-r/R/definition-emit-sql.R#L584-L620).

Found by running the corpus definition `nullable date shift` on Snowflake, with the live tests in #434.

title: Python can't query a Snowflake table whose name is lowercase
description:
On Snowflake, the Python package can't query a table created with a quoted lowercase name, such as `"survey"`. The catalog lists the table, but every query against it fails.

[`EngineBackend.quote()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-py/src/commons/_backends.py#L109-L121) uses SQLAlchemy's `quote()`. SQLAlchemy treats an all-lowercase name as case-insensitive, so it writes `survey` without quotes. Snowflake then resolves the name to `SURVEY`, which doesn't exist. commons also reports the failure as a refusal: `The current principal is not authorized to query 'COMMONS_CI.LIVE.survey'.`

The R package quotes every identifier and passes the same live test. Found by `test_a_source_over_the_namespace_describes_every_fixture_table` in #434.

title: Division by a compound expression loses its parentheses on Snowflake and Databricks
description:
When a definition divides by a compound expression, the SQL for Snowflake and Databricks drops the parentheses around the divisor. The DuckDB SQL is correct.

| Definition | SQL for Snowflake and Databricks |
|---|---|
| `amount / (ratio * 2)` | `"amount" / "ratio" * 2` |
| `-(amount - 2) / (ratio + 1.0)` | `-("amount" - 2) / "ratio" + 1.0` |

The first query runs and returns a wrong value, with no error. The second fails with `Division by zero` when `ratio` is 0, because the zero check tests `ratio + 1.0` but the query divides by `ratio`.

Both packages have the same fault: [`_divide()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-py/src/commons/_definitions/_emit_sql.py#L323-L343) and [`definition_sql_divide()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-r/R/definition-emit-sql.R#L382-L423) render both operands at the lowest precedence, then join them with `/`. `definition-warehouse-sql.json` has no case with a compound divisor, so neither suite finds this without a live warehouse. Found by `test_the_emitted_definition_sql_agrees_with_duckdb` in #434.

title: Loading dictionary without all of the required fields doesn't produce an error in `data_source` function

title: `describe_table` should describe tables outside the data source in Python
description:
Same thing as #469, but for the Python side.

In the R package, #470 lets `describe_table` describe any table the connection can query, not just the data source's tables, so it agrees with `run_sql`. Python's `_describe_table_text()` still raises when a table isn't in `source.table_ids`, so the agent can query a table it found with `run_sql` but can't describe it.

To match R:

- Describe tables outside the data source, with a note that no documentation covers them. On Snowflake and Databricks, run the usual access check first.
- Keep refusing them in trusted-only mode.
- Resolve alternate names for data source tables (`main.sales` for `sales`) to the table's label, so its documentation still shows.

Pin these in `tests/shared/describe-table.json` so both suites test the same behavior.

title: `describe_table` and `run_sql` disagree about tables outside the data source
description:
`describe_table` only accepts tables in the data source, but `run_sql` passes any SQL to the connection. When the agent finds an unselected table through `run_sql`, for example by querying `information_schema`, it can't describe the table, but it can still query it:

```
✖ [describe_table]: No table named "marts.fct_orders".
  ℹ Available tables: "sales", "customers", and "schema_migrations".
-> run_sql: select ... from marts.fct_orders ...
```

Sonnet did exactly this when asked to "look around", and answered from tables the user hadn't selected. We should either make `run_sql` respect the selection, or treat the selection as a hint and let `describe_table` describe any table the connection can see. Probably the latter.

title: `describe_table` fails on SQL Server
description:
For a generic DBI connection, `describe_table` works out column types by sampling rows:

```r
sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s LIMIT %d", DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, id), n_fallback_rows)
```

T-SQL has no `LIMIT`, so this fails for every table on SQL Server:

```
✖ Incorrect syntax near '5'.
• <SQL> 'SELECT * FROM "shop"."dbo"."sales" LIMIT 5'
```

A zero-row query (`SELECT * FROM x WHERE 1 = 0`) is portable and still returns typed columns. Other backends without `LIMIT`, like Oracle, likely fail the same way.

We might need to be careful about pre-existing commons conversation histories. I _think_ the behavior there would just be that the citation wouldn't be shown when reloading an old conversation, which is fine.

title: run_r's sandbox can read and write the host's `tempdir()`
description:
Related to #404.

The worker's write roots include the host session's `tempdir()`, only because callr puts its per-call result files there. 

https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/ed65673d5341beb771b2ee26763c6dab5272ae96/pkg-r/inst/worker/worker.R#L450-L451

So sandboxed code can read any file the host session keeps there. It can also plant a symlink where the host will later write, and the host writes through it to a path outside the sandbox. A smart model could use this maliciously—one possible example is seeing other conversations' code and results that share the same process.

callr recently (>= 3.8.0) introduced `CALLR_TMPDIR`, which we could use to give each worker its own result folder and let us drop `tempdir()` from the roots. 

(This applies regardless of Landlock, `userns`, or Seatbelt.)

title: Make calculations transparent and reproducible
description:
Some initial thoughts.

Make calculations, trusted or custom, sufficiently transparent and reproducible (or at least rerunnable) for both the app user and the app author. The app user and the app author probably need different levels and types of transparency and reproducibility.

I'm thinking that, for the app user, transparency is more important than actual reproducibility. This is already mostly addressed with #216. I think the main thing missing is consistently showing which named data source or sources contributed to a trusted calculation.

For app authors, commons should provide an ordered calculation script containing the resolved calculation code (trusted calculation code, queries, and model-authored code) needed to recreate an answer. The app author remains responsible for authenticating to the data sources. There are two situations:

- The app has trajectory logging turned on. Most of the information needed to generate the script is already recorded in the trajectories, and commons could use it to generate the script. I think this is the primary case.
  - To make the script complete, commons would need to record additional replay information alongside the existing tool calls, including the actual data source(s) used, SQL after definitions have been expanded or compiled, measure and helper source code, and any external objects the generated script would still require.
- A secondary situation is if trajectory logging is turned off, but the app author or someone else wants to get the full reproducible code from the agent's answer. This should be available upon request within the app interface, provided the current or restored conversation turns are still available. This would be useful for one-off debugging or figuring out exactly how an answer was reached.

I am uncertain about whether the generated script should be standalone or require access to the original commons layers and functions that resolve constructs like data-dictionary SQL. I think it should probably be standalone and not depend on the original commons agent for a couple reasons: I think that will actually be simpler for the app author to use, in some cases simpler for commons to generate, it's better for transparency, and it won't break if the commons layers change.  

Rerunning the script does not guarantee identical results because the underlying data may have changed.

Related:

#91
#316

title: Interoperability with other coding agents
description:
A few thoughts from discussions with folks on what the integration point is for existing coding agents that have the ability to run arbitrary code but not necessarily trusted calculations / context.

The integration point is probably _not_ commons-as-a-subagent. Sharing provider credentials between the main agent and the commons subagent seems painful and this would also limit the flow of Actual Data Objects between the main agent and the commons subagent.

So, likely, the entry point is "just" the trusted code and context. Can we make that information available to an otherwise "complete" agent? There are a few considerations here:

**Does the agent have an R/Python session already?** (e.g. Posit Assistant or Canvas.) In this case, ideally, we can just put something in that R/Python session (or give an agent the ability to bring it in), and maybe a bit of prompting that allows the main agent to run code in its "usual way", but also to access trusted code and context. For example, there could be an R6 object placed inside of the session, (see #404's addition of the `trusted` object in Artifacts), like:

```r
trusted$measure("active_arr", arguments = list(...))
```

If the agent doesn't have an R/Python session already, we could possibly do the same thing in mcp-console. (Related to #391.) The agent would gain an mcp-console MCP tool that has that object pre-loaded in it. 

**Do we own the rest of the stack for that agent?** In other words, "is it Posit Assistant or Canvas"? Ideally, the integration point allows us to surface some trust UI and/or allows us to introduce something resembling the feedback loop wherever it's integrated.

title: Split the Python `Commons` agent into a commons object and an agent
description:
#414 splits R's `commons()` into two parts. `commons()` gathers the data sources, semantic layer, and context layer into an object that code can call without a model, and `agent()` builds the agent around that object. In Python, `commons.Commons` is still the agent, so the same name means different things in the two packages, and Python has no way to call trusted calculations without an agent.

This issue is to give Python the same split, with the same methods and the same deprecation path for the old call form.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written details</summary>

**What R has after #414**

- `commons(data_sources=, semantic_layer=, context_layer=)` returns an object with these methods: `search()`, `measure()`, `metrics()`, `calculation()`, `context()`, `describe()`, and `run_sql()`. The methods return plain values (data frames or text), without handles.
- `agent(client, commons=, ...)` builds the agent from that object, and the agent exposes the object as `agent$commons`.
- The old form, `commons(client, ...)`, still builds an agent, with a deprecation warning.
- `metrics(where=)` also accepts a SQL-like string (`"region = 'EMEA' AND revenue > 0"`) or unnamed triples. A value parsed from a quoted literal stays a string, so `'001'` does not become the number `1`.
- The printed object lists its tables, its measures, and the signatures of its methods. It hides the calculation methods that have nothing to run.

**Open questions for Python**

- What to call each part. `Commons` is the agent class today. One option is a new `Agent` class, with `Commons` becoming the data object. In that case, `Commons(client, ...)` can detect a `chatlas.Chat` as its first argument, warn, and return an agent, as R does.
- Where shared behaviour goes. The `where` string grammar and the method names in the search text are behaviour users can see in both packages. They belong in `tests/shared/` as fixtures, not as a copy for each language.

**Reference**

- R implementation: `pkg-r/R/commons.R` and `pkg-r/R/agent.R` in #414.
- Python agent today: `pkg-py/src/commons/_agent.py`.
- Tracked in kata as r4tp.

</details>

title: Consider removing `commons_server()` from API
description:
And using `shinychat::chat_server()` instead.

Currently, `commons_server()` does 3 things:

1. Creates a `commons_server_start` span. 
    *  Could be removed considering that Shiny already has instrumentation for the session's lifecycle?
2. Creates a conversation id. 
    * This is a hack (that I added) and can go away when we have https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/pull/343
3. "Pre-warms" the client (i.e., builds the index, etc).
    * We might want to revisit how this works, but regardless, it might be better if this was explicit rather than implicit. Essentially the (recommended) API would change from:

```R
client <- ...
commons_server("chat", client)
```

to

```R
client <- ...
client$prewarm()
chat_server("chat", client)
```

I'm not sure if it's possible today, but at least at some point it should be possible to prewarm/cache the index independently of the shiny runtime. In that case, you might not want the pre-warming at all?

title: R reports a Snowflake table that the user can't read as missing
description:
When the role has no privilege on a Snowflake table, `data_source(con, tables = ...)` says the table doesn't exist. The error is `` `tables` names table not on the connection: "COMMONS_CI.LIVE.denied_orders". ``

Snowflake hides a table from a role that has no privilege on it. So after the probe query fails, the [`dbExistsTable()` check](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/0d30ea4ffa99749dbaba90c4c767ce527e4221e0/pkg-r/R/data-source.R#L1030-L1049) returns `FALSE` and R reports a missing table. `catalog_probe_relation()` classifies the same failure as an authorization refusal, and the Python package raises its authorization error for it. A user who needs to ask for access is told instead that the table doesn't exist. Found by "live Snowflake classifies denied query access" in #431.

title: describe_table summarizes a five-row sample with the shape of a whole-table profile
description: `describe_table` samples five rows (`SAMPLE_ROWS` in `pkg-py/src/commons/_tools.py`, `n_sample` in `pkg-r/R/data-source.R`) and then summarizes them with `ellmer::df_schema()` (and something else on the Python side). We shouldn't be computing those summaries on the sample. Currently, we get around this by telling the model that the summaries are being computed on a subset of the data and not to read into them too much, but we really shouldn't be computing them in the first place. At the same time, it's nice if we can describe the table enough that we can write code against it. What does the model have access to already? If that's enough, should we just remove that line (and the prompting associated with it)?

title: Measures-only mode?
description:
Cross-posting from https://github.com/posit-dev/clinical-trials-agent/issues/7.

Would you be willing to consider an optional way to restrict the tool set to just user-defined measures? If the user opts in, the [security and governance](https://posit-dev.github.io/commons/articles/governance.html) issues automatically disappear, and the agent can easily follow [strict trusted mini-agent rules](https://trustedminiagents.dev).

With [`clinical-trials-agent`](https://github.com/posit-dev/clinical-trials-agent) specifically, my team and I usually need to restrict the set of analyses to ones we trust, and not let the agent write custom analysis code. Analyses are almost always pre-specified in a statistical analysis plan (SAP), and we have formal standards to run them. Analysts are in a hurry and need to run hundreds of these, and I would have a hard time having confidence in most users to pause and think about the different levels of trust of the results.

title: Connect previews should run the pull request's code, for R and Python
description:
Pull requests that change `pkg-r/` deploy a preview of the R demo app to Connect ([`deploy.yml`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/.github/workflows/deploy.yml)), but that preview does not run the pull request's R code. Connect installs packages from the committed [`manifest.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/pkg-r/inst/manifest.json), which pins `commons` to a commit from 2026-08-25 and `ellmer` to 0.4.2. Python has no preview at all.

This issue covers both:

- **R:** generate the manifest from the pull request's checkout at deploy time instead of committing it, and pass a model to `chat_anthropic()` in [`app.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/pkg-r/inst/app.R).
- **Python:** deploy [`pkg-py/demo.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/pkg-py/demo.py) the same way, installing `commons` from the checkout and not from PyPI.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

- The unpinned model changes behavior. ellmer 0.4.2 defaults `chat_anthropic()` to `claude-sonnet-4-6`, and 0.5.0 defaults it to `claude-sonnet-5`. When asked to sleep with `run_r` before it plots, Sonnet 4.6 skipped the sleep in 6 of 6 trials, and Sonnet 5 called it in 6 of 6. That is why the deployed app and a local run disagree.
- Python needs new content items on dev and staging for the `main` deploys, and the provider credentials on Connect. `demo.py` gets its model from `chatlas.ChatAuto`.
- [`connect-previews-cleanup.yml`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/.github/workflows/connect-previews-cleanup.yml) runs for every closed pull request, but its name starts with "R:". Make sure it also removes the Python previews, and rename it.
- Name the deploy target explicitly in each step, as the R steps do. Two steps that deploy from one directory broke staging in #318.
- Tracked in kata as `rnzp`.

</details>

title: making commons data structures / tools available to external agents
description:
## The flow of data in commons

commons takes in:

* Data sources (DBI connections, tables, pins)
    - Sometimes with a data dictionary attached
* Semantic layer
    - Sometimes R code in a .R file, with sufficient docs to create an ellmer::tool
    - Sometimes built from elements of the data dictionary
* Context layer
    - Literally whatever free text

All of the above gets chunked up, with subsets included in the system prompt and tools:

* `search_pool()`: discover entries in the semantic layer
* `call_measure()` / `call_metric()`: call entries in the semantic layer
* `describe_table()`: HEAD on the table / relevant entries from the data dict
* `search_context()`: search inside of the semantic layer and context layer
* `run_sql()`: query the DB with free-handed SQL
* `run_r()`: (sandboxed) code execution, with `run_sql()` outputs serialized into the session

## Interoperability with coding agents / commons

Some (notably, Canvas and Posit Assistant) MCP consumers have a code execution tool already.

The story here depends on whether we want to serve the end user or serve the data scientist that makes the agent.

Some options:

* MCP, with all tools

title: R CMD check on macos-latest fails to extract mac.cran.dev's odbc binary
description:
The `macos-latest (release)` job in R CMD check fails while it installs dependencies. pak downloads the odbc 1.7.1 binary from `mac.cran.dev`, and that file is Zstandard data with a `.tgz` name, so pak stops with "unknown archive type". CRAN has a valid gzip binary of the same build.

#389 works around this. It installs odbc from CRAN before pak runs, and pak keeps that copy.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written detail: verification</summary>

- Posit Package Manager has no odbc binary for macOS arm64 and R 4.6. The file returns 404 and the `PACKAGES` index has no odbc entry, so pak resolves odbc from `cran.rstudio.com`, with `mac.cran.dev` as the second source.
- `cran.r-project.org` and `cran.rstudio.com` serve a gzip file whose MD5 matches their `PACKAGES` index.
- `mac.cran.dev` lists the same MD5 in its own `PACKAGES` index, but the file it serves has a different MD5.
- The failure is repeatable. Both CI runs on 2026-09-23 failed the same way (on `main` after #385, and on #389 before its current approach), and a local run on R 4.6.1 arm64 with a fresh library reproduces it. In each pak log, the downloaded file is the 3.24 MB `mac.cran.dev` file, not the 3.81 MB CRAN file.
- The cache bump in #385 did not change the result.

</details>

title: `coerce_arg()` cannot validate a non-enum array argument: `Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values`
description:
## Summary

A measure whose argument is an array of plain strings (or numbers, integers, booleans) is
uncallable. `commons:::coerce_arg()` applies the enum-only `values` property lookup to the array's
`items` type, so validation errors before the measure is ever reached. The model's *correct* tool
call is rejected by the harness and comes back to it as `Tool calling failed with error Can't find
property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values`, which it typically responds to by retrying.

## Environment

- commons 0.1.0 (CRAN)
- ellmer 0.5.0
- S7 0.2.2
- R 4.5.0 (2025-04-11 ucrt), Windows 11

## Reproducible example

No data, no database and no LLM required.

```r
library(ellmer)

arr <- function(items) ellmer::tool(
  function(x) x,
  name        = "demo",
  description = "A measure with an array argument.",
  arguments   = list(x = ellmer::type_array(items))
)

# enum[] -- validates fine
str(commons:::validate_measure_args(arr(type_enum(values = c("a", "b"))),
                                    list(x = c("a", "b"))))

# string[] -- e.g. `@param indicators `string[]`` on a chart measure
str(commons:::validate_measure_args(arr(type_string()),
                                    list(x = c("a", "b"))))
```

Actual output (verbatim, an unrelated build-version warning trimmed):

```
List of 1
 $ x: chr [1:2] "a" "b"
Error: Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values
Execution halted
```

Expected: the second call returns `List of 1 / $ x: chr [1:2] "a" "b"` as well — an array of plain
strings has no value set to test membership against, so there is nothing to validate.

`validate_measure_args()` is the function `call_measure_tool()` calls, so this is the live path and
not an artefact of reaching for an internal:

```
call_measure (tool)  ->  commons:::call_measure_tool()
                     ->  commons:::validate_measure_args()
                     ->  commons:::coerce_arg()
```

Every non-enum item type fails identically:

```
string[]  -> ERROR: Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values
number[]  -> ERROR: Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values
integer[] -> ERROR: Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values
boolean[] -> ERROR: Can't find property <ellmer::TypeBasic>@values
```

## Cause

`coerce_arg()` (commons 0.1.0):

```r
kind <- type_kind(type)
if (kind %in% c("enum", "array")) {
  allowed <- if (kind == "enum") {
    type_values(type)
  } else {
    type_values(S7::prop(type, "items"))   # <-- unconditional
  }
  bad <- setdiff(as.character(value), allowed)
  ...
}
```

`type_values()` is `S7::prop(type, "values")`. That property exists on `ellmer::TypeEnum` and not on
`ellmer::TypeBasic`, so the array branch throws for any array whose `items` is a basic type.

The sibling helper in the same package guards the identical lookup:

```r
array_items_label <- function(items) {
  if (identical(type_kind(items), "enum")) {
    paste(type_values(items), collapse = ", ")
  } else {
    type_kind(items)
  }
}
```

So `array_items_label()` already encodes the correct rule; `coerce_arg()` omits it.

## Consequence

Any measure with an array-of-basic-type argument is uncallable through `call_measure`. In our
agent, four measure arguments are `string[]` (e.g. an `indicators: string[]` overlay argument on a
chart measure), and those measures were rejected on every attempt.

Two things make it expensive to diagnose from the outside:

1. The failure is attributed to the model. The tool result the model receives is a generic S7
   property error with no argument name in it, so it reads as a bad call rather than as a harness
   defect. Measured on one item: the model emitted exactly the intended arguments —
   `{"ticker":"AAPL","days":730,"indicators":["sma:200"]}` — and got the error back.
2. The retry is unbounded and grows the conversation. The model re-searches the measure pool, gets
   the same roster back, and tries again; in our case the conversation reached 17 near-identical
   search results (~121 KB, 89% of the request body) and then hit the server's context ceiling as
   an HTTP 400. Two different-looking transport 400s upstream of this both trace back to this one
   branch.

An open grammar such as `"sma:200"` could not be enumerated even in principle, so the membership
test is not merely unavailable here — it is not meaningful.

## Suggested fix

Guard the membership test on the item type actually having a value set, mirroring
`array_items_label()`, and coerce array elements by their item kind rather than always to
character. (Today the array branch ends in `return(as.character(value))`, so even once the
membership test is fixed a `number[]` argument would reach the measure as a character vector — a
second, smaller defect on the same branch.)

```r
if (kind == "array") {
  items <- S7::prop(type, "items")
  if (identical(type_kind(items), "enum")) {
    bad <- setdiff(as.character(value), type_values(items))
    if (length(bad)) {
      cli::cli_abort(...)
    }
    return(as.character(value))
  }
  return(switch(
    type_kind(items),
    number  = as.numeric(value),
    integer = as.integer(value),
    boolean = as.logical(value),
    as.character(value)
  ))
}
```

Happy to open a PR with tests covering `string[]`, `number[]` and `enum[]` if that is useful.

title: Investigate dependencies `INFO` in R CMD check
description:
Currently: ``` * checking package dependencies ... INFO Imports includes 26 non-default packages. Importing from so many packages makes the package vulnerable to any of them becoming unavailable. Move as many as possible to Suggests and use conditionally. ``` Worth investigating whether we can drive this down to 20.
Write-up from Codex

I count 26 non-base Imports in the current `DESCRIPTION`—27 including base package `utils`. The reported 25 likely came from a nearby snapshot. Counts below are runtime namespace references in `R/`; comments, examples, and tests are excluded. | Package | Uses / files | Assessment | |---|---:|---| | bslib | 17 / 4 | Keep. Substantial app/reviewer UI; also required by `shinychat`. | | callr | 3 / 2 | Keep. Persistent sandbox worker and pin prewarming; difficult to replace. | | cli | 260 / 32 | Keep. Conditions throughout; required by five other Imports. | | coro | 5 / 2 | Keep. Core streaming, plus five unqualified `yield()` calls; required by `ellmer`. | | DBI | 116 / 8 | Keep. Core database interface; required by `duckdb` and `ragnar`. | | duckdb | 1 / 1 | Keep. Provides local data-frame databases; required by `ragnar` anyway. | | ellmer | 96 / 13 | Keep. Fundamental to the package. | | evaluate | 2 / 1 | Keep. Captures sandboxed R output; replacing it is difficult. Required by `knitr`. | | filelock | 2 / 1 | Strong Suggests candidate. Used only for optional pins access. | | highr | 1 / 1 | Easy to replace with unhighlighted escaped code, but `knitr` requires it. | | htmltools | 54 / 6 | Keep. Core result rendering, citations, app, and reviewer UI. | | httr2 | 35 / 1 | Keep. Only Connect operations, but both `ellmer` and `ragnar` require it. | | jsonlite | 12 / 9 | Keep. Used across several core formats; required by four other Imports. | | knitr | 2 / 1 | Possible removal, but requires writing reliable Markdown and HTML table renderers. | | later | 5 / 2 | Keep. Worker polling and scheduling; required by `ellmer` and `promises`. | | magick | 3 / 1 | Strong removal/Suggests candidate. Only downsizes plot PNGs for the model. | | processx | 1 / 1 | Keep. Needed for worker file-descriptor polling; required by `callr`. | | promises | 8 / 2 | Keep. Core asynchronous worker behavior; required by `ellmer`. | | R6 | 4 / 2 | Keep. Defines the agent and layer classes; widely transitively required. | | ragg | 1 / 1 | Plausible Suggests candidate with a base graphics fallback, at some rendering risk. | | ragnar | 11 / 1 | Keep. Implements the advertised context-search layer. | | rlang | 239 / 30, plus 171 `%\|\|%` uses | Keep. Pervasive and transitively unavoidable. | | roxygen2 | 9 / 1 | Good Suggests candidate if file-based measures may require an optional dependency. | | S7 | 36 / 10 | Keep. Core ellmer content/type handling; required by three other Imports. | | sass | 1 / 1 | Keep. Tiny direct use and already required transitively through `bslib`. | | shinychat | 10 / 4 | Keep unless intentionally creating a headless installation profile. Deeply integrated into displays, reminders, apps, and trajectory review. | | utils | 21 / 13 | Base R; irrelevant to the warning. | The best immediate candidates are: 1. `filelock` → Suggests Its complete use is essentially: ```r lock <- filelock::lock(...) on.exit(filelock::unlock(lock), add = TRUE) ``` This path exists only for pins, which is already in Suggests. Add a conditional dependency check when a pin is read. 2. `roxygen2` → Suggests It is used only when `semantic_layer()` receives file paths. The transition is mechanically easy because inline measures need none of it, and the relevant tests already call `skip_if_not_installed("roxygen2")`. The product tradeoff is that file-based measures are presented as the most straightforward workflow. 3. `magick` → Suggests or remove It only performs: ```r image_read() image_resize() image_write() ``` A fallback could send the existing high-resolution PNG to the model. That increases payload size but preserves functionality and removes a comparatively fragile system dependency. 4. `ragg` → Suggests, optionally A conditional `grDevices::png()` fallback is small, but `ragg` provides more reliable cross-platform rendering. I would remove it only if reducing compiled dependencies is a priority. A second, coherent—but more involved—change would remove `knitr` and `highr`: implement the two small table renderers locally and fall back to escaped, unhighlighted R code. This becomes worthwhile particularly if `roxygen2` also moves to Suggests. Nineteen of the 26 non-base Imports are already dependencies of another Import. The strongest unavoidable clusters are: ```text ellmer -> cli, coro, httr2, jsonlite, later, promises, R6, rlang, S7 ragnar -> cli, DBI, duckdb, httr2, jsonlite, rlang, S7 shinychat -> bslib, cli, coro, ellmer, htmltools, jsonlite, promises, R6, rlang, S7 -> bslib -> sass roxygen2 -> cli, knitr, R6, rlang -> knitr -> evaluate, highr callr -> processx, R6 ``` Only seven are roots within the current direct-import graph: ```text callr, filelock, magick, ragg, ragnar, roxygen2, shinychat ``` Of those, only `filelock`, `magick`, and `ragg` are isolated, narrow-purpose additions. Those are where dependency reduction most directly reduces availability risk. I would not move transitively available packages to Suggests merely to silence the check. Their current availability is an implementation detail of another package and can change. The honest near-term reduction is `filelock` and `roxygen2`, with `magick` likely removable via fallback; everything else either supports a central feature or adds no independent availability risk.

title: Support shinychat history for composed Chatlas clients such as Python Commons
description:
For Python only, when using commons with page_chat, the conversation history feature doesn't work; it's always blank.

Python `Commons` deliberately composes a `chatlas.Chat` rather than subclassing it. It exposes Chatlas-compatible behavior:

- `stream_async(...)`
- `get_turns() -> list[chatlas.Turn]`
- `set_turns(Sequence[chatlas.Turn])`

This allows shinychat to stream from a Commons agent directly.

However, shinychat recognizes Chatlas turn history using a nominal check equivalent to:

```python
isinstance(client, chatlas.Chat)
```

Other clients follow the generic `ClientWithTurns` path, which expects JSON-round-trippable turns. Commons therefore falls into the generic path even though its history uses `chatlas.Turn` semantics.

The result is that direct streaming works, but shinychat's conversation history and New Chat support require an application-level adapter that converts:

```text
chatlas.Turn <-> JSON dictionaries
```

For example, the desired integration is roughly:

```python
agent = Commons(...)
chat = shinychat.Chat("chat", client=agent)
ui = shinychat.page_chat("chat", history=True)
```

without needing a wrapper solely for history serialization.

History restoration also needs to call `Commons.queue_restore_reminder()`, similar to the hook installed by R's `commons_server()`.

## Possible directions

Some possible fixes:

- Have shinychat or chatlas define an explicit protocol or capability for clients whose history uses `chatlas.Turn`.
- Give clients explicit JSON history serialization/deserialization methods.
- Standardize one history representation across shinychat clients.
- Add a Python integration helper analogous to R's `commons_server()`.

title: Iterating on and maintaining the agent
description:
Thinking about the refinement / maintenance experience.

Once the initial draft of the agent is working, how can a data scientist test out the app interactively and improve it along the way? Then, once deployed, interactions with commons agents will produce a lot of data. That data will be tagged with measures of trustworthiness for each response. How can we help the data scientist make use of those responses tagged as untrustworthy to improve the agent?

One possible view of this is a Shiny app in which the data scientist is very involved with refining the `commons()` agent. In that case, I think there's the agent app itself on the LHS (possibly with some pre-loaded conversation history) and some sort of feedback intake or refinement UI on the RHS? And then the data scientist either asks questions of their own or "loads in" some pool of conversations from live conversations that were tagged as untrustworthy, and provides feedback manually.

Another view of this world is that this process is semi-automated by an agent (probably the users' coding agent of choice). In this world, the refinement process is just an agent skill that has Codex or Claude Code or Posit Assistant load in all of this data, read the transcripts itself, then extract themes / propose refinements to the context layer (and _maybe_ the semantic layer).

Evals are certainly part of this process as well. Either of those entry points should probably include a vitals-based eval being constructed (or ran against) as a byproduct.

title: consider paring back OTel UX code
description:
Currently, `commons::commons(log = TRUE)` sets some environmental variables and then subsets into `ellmer:::otel_cache_tracer()` to refresh the OTel tracing code. 

This makes _local_ tracing a bit more convenient (but is likely not CRAN-compliant). I'm not that worried about the local case and am fine to remove all of that in favor of noting in the onboarding flow that users should set them and restart R.

Without us doing this `log` trickery, on Connect, these variables will mostly be set appropriately automatically. That said, the user would still need to set `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` in a `.Rprofile` and then restart R (so that `ellmer:::otel_cache_tracer()` runs on ellmer package load) in order to deploy their app with tracing enabled. **This is more cumbersome than I'd like—it doesn't seem like you should have to edit your .Rprofile and restart your R session to do this**—but I don't see a way to make this 'just work' for users other than setting that envvar ourselves and then re-running `ellmer:::otel_cache_tracer()`. Ideally, ellmer could give us some entry point to refresh that setup.

(In the short term, we do still need to do this hacky subsetting for the OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES hotfix #66, but we can remove that by the time 0.1.0 is released.)

A measure argument's declared type is silently ignored once its `@param` description occupies more than one physical line. The enum below is read as a free-text `string`, with the raw type span left in the description the model sees.

title: Provenance marker is lost when an answer ends with a table
description:
The provenance marker disappears when a model's answer ends with a markdown table. Both packages (R and Python) are affected. Nothing errors, so the answer simply reaches the reader unclassified. I ran across this while testing the Python UI and noticed the "verified icon" was missing sometimes. I was able to narrow it down to only happening in the case when the answer ends with a table. The agent returns the provenance marker, but it's not getting rendered properly by the UI. Compare this result, where the agent added a text summary line after the table: With this one, where I told it not to: shinychat attaches an aside to the markdown block it sits in. Both packages append `` as a trailing chunk with no block of its own ([`pkg-r/R/commons.R:409`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/pkg-r/R/commons.R#L409), [`pkg-py/src/commons/_agent.py:287`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/main/pkg-py/src/commons/_agent.py#L287)). After a paragraph it lands inline and renders. After a table there is no block to attach to, the aside never reaches the DOM, and a small stray artifact of an empty `` row is left at the bottom of the table. I confirmed this behavior in both R and Python.
Agent-written detail: how this was isolated Four runs against Bedrock Sonnet, one boundary at a time. **The agent emits the aside correctly.** Streaming outside any UI yields a final chunk of `…`, with `collect_appended_tags()` returning `[Tag.A]`. Every icon file returns 200 from the served bundle. The markup and the icon URL are correct, so the loss is at the browser. **Answer ending in a paragraph.** Pill renders, label `Verified answer`, `trusted-icon.svg` in the DOM, last block `P`. **Answer ending in a table.** Last block `TABLE`, no pill, and the string `shiny-aside` is not in the DOM at all, so the markdown renderer consumed it rather than leaving it as inert markup. In R the same run shows "Ran a trusted calculation" in the trace, so the tag was A and the markup was produced. **One run showed no pill for a different and correct reason.** No data tool ran in that exchange, so `derive_provenance_tag()` returned `None`, which is the documented "no pill at all" case. Worth noting so it is not mistaken for this bug. Both client bundles carry the same aside-parsing regex even though R ships shinychat 0.4.0.9000 and Python ships 0.7.0, which is why one root cause produces the same symptom in both. shinychat documents an aside as "a small pill that appears at the end of the paragraph or list item it's attached to", created by "an inline `` tag anywhere in a block's markdown". The packages do not give it a block. A likely fix is to emit the aside as its own block when the answer does not end in an attachable one, rather than always inline. That changes marker placement, which is why it belongs in a shared fixture. > Tracked locally in kata as `g6vz`.

title: R CMD check is red on main: shinychat now refuses chat$clear() when history is enabled
description:
`R CMD check` is failing on `main` with one test error:

```
Error ('test-chat.R:63:7'): commons_server queues a restore reminder when history is restored
Error in `chat$clear()`: Can't clear a chat with conversation history enabled. Use `chat$new_chat()` to start a new conversation.
```

CI resolves shinychat from r-universe (`shinychat_0.4.0.9000_dde163e`) rather than a pinned version, so a development build changed under us.

[shinychat #399](https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/pull/399) ("Add new_chat for conversation history"), commit [`dde163e`](https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/commit/dde163ea6b27099304a658f3649dd1fac98208bd), merged 2026-09-08 and added `new_chat()` along with a guard at the top of `client_clear()` in `pkg-r/R/chat_app.R`: when a history controller exists, `clear()` now aborts instead of clearing.

In commons, `shinychat::chat_server()` defaults to `history = TRUE`, and `commons_server()` calls it without passing `history` (`pkg-r/R/chat.R:116`), so there is no configuration reachable through commons in which `clear()` still works. `clear()` is not deprecated, it is closed off for the only setup this package creates. This needs a decision about the test rather than a rename.

The test uses `clear()` at line 63 to assert that the pending restore reminder is dropped, then separately asserts the same thing through `controller$new_chat()` two lines later.

Deciding what the test should assert is an R behavior question. The options look like: 
- exercise the clear path with history disabled, since that is now the only configuration where `clear()` is reachable
- or drop the `clear()` assertion because `new_chat()` already covers the same commons behaviour
- or keep asserting that commons drops the reminder and accept that upstream now owns which method gets there.

It's also worth a decision whether commons CI should pin the shinychat build it resolves, given upstream changes can cause CI failures unexpectedly (like this one).

@simonpcouch @cpsievert any thoughts?

title: Inherited ellmer methods answer without the turn rules or a provenance marker
description:
`Commons` inherits from `ellmer::Chat` ([commons.R:213-215](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/d1833b2fdf2bbbe2d3ac37b345d914992cb320b5/pkg-r/R/commons.R#L213-L215)) and overrides only two of the six methods that can produce an answer. `chat()` and `stream_async()` are overridden. `stream()`, `chat_async()`, `chat_structured()` and `chat_structured_async()` are inherited without change.

This means that if a user constructs a `Commons` instance and uses one of those inherited methods, they don't get any of the commons-y goodness, since the turn rules never run. `stream()` and `chat_async()` skip the turn reminder, the restore reminder, and the conversation-turn span, which `chat()` installs at [commons.R:309-318](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/d1833b2fdf2bbbe2d3ac37b345d914992cb320b5/pkg-r/R/commons.R#L309-L318). They also skip the citation scan and the provenance aside, which only `stream_async()` adds. An answer from `commons$stream()` therefore reaches the reader with no provenance marker and no verified citations, and the trajectory record for that turn has no span.

This is probably worth consideration if we want to support those other methods, or (if not) should we prohibit them from being used in Commons? 

Two parts of this are worth separating:

- `stream()` and `chat_async()` produce prose for a person to read. These are the methods that need the turn rules.
- `chat_structured()` and `chat_structured_async()` return parsed data. A provenance marker appended to their output would make the JSON invalid, so the correct behavior for them is probably to abort with a message that names `stream_async()`, not to scan.

This is an artifact of inheriting directly from ellmer on the R side. The Python package instead composes an object from chatlas instead of inheriting from it, so we're using an object that we explicitly provide methods on. The underlying chatlas client is reachable only through the documented `client` attribute, which cleraly documents that it skips the scanner and the marker. Composition makes the marked path the only path. Inheritance makes it a subset of the surface, and the subset needs a new override every time ellmer adds a method.

This came up while building the Python chat adapter for the UI layer, and I figured it was worth opening an issue for consideration.

@simonpcouch

title: deploy job fails: rsconnect-python 1.31.0 rejects the staging deploy
description:
The `deploy` job fails on every pull request and will fail on the next `main` push that touches `pkg-r/**`. The "Deploy to Connect (staging)" step stops with:

> Error: This directory has been deployed before, but the server it was last deployed to, \*\*\*, is no longer saved, so the target has to be named. Pass -n/--name, -s/--server, or --connect-cloud with -A/--account, to say where to deploy.

The "Deploy to Connect (dev)" step succeeds. Only staging fails.

## Cause

`rsconnect-python` 1.31.0 was published to PyPI at 2026-09-08 19:49 UTC. `posit-cli` 0.1.1 requires `rsconnect-python>=1.30,<2`, and `posit-dev/connect-actions/deploy` installs it fresh on every run, so the new version arrived with no change in this repository.

The workflow runs two deploy steps in one job, and both use `path: pkg-r/inst`. The dev step deploys and saves a deployment record into that directory ("Saving deployed information..."), then it removes the saved server nickname when it exits. The staging step then reads that record, which names a server that is no longer saved. Earlier versions of rsconnect-python accepted this. 1.31.0 refuses and asks for an explicit target.

The workflow has always depended on rsconnect-python being lenient here. The new release removed that leniency.

## Timeline

| Time (UTC) | Event | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 18:42 | deploy run ([logs](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/actions/runs/34264674312)) | pass |
| 19:28 | deploy run | pass |
| 19:49 | rsconnect-python 1.31.0 published | |
| 20:09 | deploy run ([logs](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/actions/runs/34273119846)) | fail |
| 20:15 | re-run of the failed job | fail |
| 20:46 | deploy run ([logs](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/actions/runs/34276712859)) | fail |

## What this is not

- Not a code change in this repository. The failing tree differs from a passing tree only in prompt and tool-description text.
- Not the action. `posit-dev/connect-actions@main` is unpinned, but its last commit is 2026-08-28.
- Not the CLI. Both the passing and failing runs installed `posit-cli==0.1.1`.
- Not the secrets. `CONNECT_SERVER_DEV` and `CONNECT_SERVER_STAGING` were last updated 2026-08-05.
- Not the workflow structure on its own. In the passing run the dev step also saved a record, and staging still succeeded.

One thing is inference rather than fact: I did not read the 1.31.0 diff, because its changelog was not reachable through the API. The timing and the error text point at that release. To confirm it, pin `rsconnect-python==1.30.0` and run the job again.

## Options

1. Pin `rsconnect-python` to 1.30.x for the deploy job. This is the fastest way to get CI green, and it confirms the diagnosis.
2. Give the staging step an explicit target with `-s` or `-n` through `rsconnect-args`. The step already passes `content-guid`, so the target is known.
3. Give each deploy step its own copy of `pkg-r/inst`, so the two steps do not share a deployment record.

Option 1 or 2 unblocks CI. The durable fix belongs upstream in `posit-dev/connect-actions`, which can constrain the dependency or name the server for each deploy.

Found while working on #317, whose other 12 checks pass.

title: R reads a three-part table name string as a dotted schema instead of catalog.schema.table
description:
## Bug

In R, `data_source(con, tables = "ANALYTICS.PUBLIC.ORDERS")` folds everything before the last dot into the schema: `DBI::Id(schema = "ANALYTICS.PUBLIC", table = "ORDERS")`. Quoted, that is `"ANALYTICS.PUBLIC"."ORDERS"` — one identifier with a dot inside it, naming a schema no warehouse has. The zero-row probe then fails and `data_source()` errors with a "table does not exist" for a table that does.

```r
id <- DBI::Id(schema = "ANALYTICS.PUBLIC", table = "ORDERS")
DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(DBI::ANSI(), id)
#> <SQL> "ANALYTICS.PUBLIC"."ORDERS"
```

The fold dates to 97db857 ("support schema-qualified connection tables", closes #15), written before the package had any catalog support. Catalogs arrived later via `DBI::Id(catalog = ...)` objects (the Snowflake/Databricks work), and the string parser was never revisited.

R also accepts `"a.b.c.d"`, folding it into a doubly-dotted schema.

## Expected

Match the behavior #274 gives the Python side:

- `"catalog.schema.table"` → `DBI::Id(catalog = ..., schema = ..., table = ...)`
- More than three parts → an error naming the input and pointing at `DBI::Id` for literal names containing dots
- One and two parts behave as today

The workaround meanwhile is an explicit `DBI::Id(catalog = "ANALYTICS", schema = "PUBLIC", table = "ORDERS")`.

## Shared contract

Table-name parsing is user-observable behavior both packages expose through `tables`, so the parsing rules belong in `tests/shared/` as an executable fixture read by both suites. The fixture cannot land until R is fixed, because R currently fails the three-part case. Being fixed in #274.

title: Run the warehouse implementations against real Snowflake and Databricks
description:
Everything commons knows about Snowflake and Databricks has been verified against a fake. Nothing in `pkg-py` has ever run a statement against a real warehouse, and the R live tests have no way to run anywhere except one person's laptop. The catalog readers, the access and session checks, and the warehouse SQL emitters are all specified against what we believe those systems return.

## What exists today

`pkg-r/tests/testthat/test-live-warehouses.R` (744 lines) plus `helper-live-warehouses.R` connect through ODBC (`odbc::snowflake()`, a DSN named `Databricks`) and skip unless R options name real objects: a test table, a denied table, an alternate Snowflake role, semantic views, parameterized models. `pkg-r/tests/testthat/README.md` documents the options. Nothing provisions the objects those options point at, no CI job runs any of it, and `pkg-py` has no equivalent at all: every warehouse test there drives a fake backend that replays canned rows.

## The open question

Where does the warehouse come from? This is the decision the rest depends on, so it should be made first. Options worth pricing:

- a shared Posit-owned Snowflake account and Databricks workspace, with credentials in GitHub secrets;
- per-developer trial accounts plus a provisioning script;
- Databricks free edition or a Snowflake trial, created and torn down in CI;
- accepting that this stays manual, and lives in a documented pre-release checklist rather than in CI.

## Then the mechanics

- **Provisioning as code.** The fixtures are not just a table. The access tests need an object the test principal genuinely cannot read, and the session test needs a second usable role. A SQL script (or Terraform) that creates the schema, tables, views, roles, and grants would bring any account to a known state and stop the test options being hand-typed identifiers.
- **A Python harness of the same shape.** Python connects through SQLAlchemy rather than ODBC/DBI, so this needs `snowflake-sqlalchemy` and `databricks-sqlalchemy` as optional dev dependencies, an environment-variable or config equivalent of the R options, and a clean skip when they are unset.
- **Credential handling.** What reaches CI, what stays local, and what a contributor without warehouse access sees. Today they get a clean skip, which should stay true.
- **Scope of what gets asserted.** Prefer what a fake cannot tell us over restating unit tests: identifier case folding per backend, the real row shapes of `SHOW OBJECTS`, `DESC TABLE`, `system.information_schema` and `DESCRIBE TABLE`, the SQLSTATE and message a genuine permission refusal carries, the session identity queries, and whether the Snowflake and Databricks SQL the definition emitters produce actually executes.

## Why it matters

`tests/shared/catalog-access-errors.json` decides whether a driver failure is an authorization refusal, a transient fault, or neither, and commons caches the refusal or retries based on that answer. Its cases were written from documentation rather than from a captured failure. `tests/shared/definition-warehouse-sql.json` pins SQL that no warehouse has ever parsed, and it is hand-maintained precisely because there is no upstream authority to check it against. A live run is what turns both from plausible into verified. The same applies to the native semantic-model probes for Snowflake semantic views and Databricks metric views, which cannot be written honestly without one.

Not urgent for the conference demo, which runs on DuckDB, and not a blocker for the data layer milestone. It is what stands between "the warehouse support is implemented" and "the warehouse support is known to work".

title: Consider reintroducing `commons_ui()`
description:
Right now, we've managed to fit in the UI changes from commons into `commons_theme()`. 

In the future, commons will support an Artifacts-style feature, where users can compose Quarto documents and Shiny dashboards and then one-click share them on Connect.

This sort of feature wouldn't fit into the `commons_theme()` API. I'm wondering whether we should reintroduce `commons_ui()` so that we are able to control as much as we need to to implement the features that we want to. That way, when we ship artifacts, we don't need users to make any changes to customize their calls to `page_chat()`--it "just works."

---

This is admittedly a less general, composable, customizable stance than shiny, shinychat, or querychat might make, but leans more towards the "just works" stance that this package tries to take: bring your understanding of how to analyze your data and we'll bring the harness and a modern, deploy-ready chat app. #155 also feels related here on the "it's just an ellmer Chat" thread—for now, we're not exporting tools / broadly allowing customization of the harness.

title: Consider a persistent, shareable context index
description:
Split out from #171 discussion.

The context index behind `search_context` is an in-memory ragnar store (`context_store()` in `pkg-r/R/context-layer.R`), so every process — including every Shiny session's agent — rebuilds it from scratch. `prewarm_context()` can move that cost off the first question, but it can't be done offline or shared across sessions.

If the build cost ever becomes worth avoiding, the move is a persistent ragnar store (`location =`) keyed by a hash of the layer's docs, which would allow:

* building the index offline ahead of deployment,
* sharing one index across Shiny sessions.

Current thinking: BM25-only builds (`embed = NULL`, no embedding calls) are cheap enough that the hash-invalidation and store-location complexity hasn't been justified. Revisit if measurement shows the build is a real startup cost (e.g. large context layers), or if embeddings are ever introduced.

title: test in parallel
run_r leaks later timers, which stalls the R test suite for ten minutes
description:
`R CMD check` on `pkg-r/` spends about ten minutes idle. [Run 33796849087](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/actions/runs/33796849087/job/100786518215) took 15m22s, and the `checking tests` step was 11m25s of that. Check reports the split itself:

```
Running 'testthat.R' [2m/11m]
```

Two minutes of CPU, eleven minutes of wall clock. Every other check step takes a few seconds. The same stall happens locally, where the suite looks hung on `test-trajectory-review.R`.

## Cause

`shiny::testServer()` reads an output through `MockShinySession$getOutput()`, which calls `shiny:::extract()` and then `shiny:::wait_for_it()`:

```r
wait_for_it <- function() {
  while (!later::loop_empty()) later::run_now(0.1)
}
```

That does not wait for the output's own promise. It waits until the whole global `later` queue is empty, so anything left on the queue has to fire first.

`run_r_tool()` leaves things on that queue. Every call ends in [`schedule_worker_reap()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/76f9e38edcf42a19e86245a05f8740ee342e5793/pkg-r/R/run-r.R#L433), which arms a timer at `commons.run_r_idle_timeout + 1`, 601 seconds by default. Each call also arms a timeout timer in [`worker_await()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/76f9e38edcf42a19e86245a05f8740ee342e5793/pkg-r/R/run-r.R#L471) at `commons.run_r_timeout`, 60 seconds by default. Neither is cancelled when the call settles, and `worker_close()` does not cancel them either.

So `test-run-r.R` finishes in ten seconds and hands the global loop 70 pending callbacks. `test-trajectory-review.R` then reads `output$entries` inside a `testServer()` block ([test-trajectory-review.R#L297](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/76f9e38edcf42a19e86245a05f8740ee342e5793/pkg-r/tests/testthat/test-trajectory-review.R#L297)), and that read cannot return until the last 601 second timer fires.

## Measurements

Immediately after `test-run-r.R`, the global loop holds 70 callbacks in two clusters: 34 at 46 to 60 seconds, and 35 at 587 to 601 seconds. The two clusters match the two option defaults. The farthest is 600.9 seconds out, and draining the loop the way `wait_for_it()` does takes 600.9 seconds.

Running `test-run-r.R` and then `test-trajectory-review.R` in one session, the test "the viewer filters conversations and follows selection" takes 601.1 seconds. With `commons.run_r_idle_timeout = 2` and `commons.run_r_timeout = 2`, the same test takes 3.1 seconds. A bisect over every other test file shows `test-run-r.R` is the only one that triggers this. Run on its own, the whole suite is about 40 seconds.

A stack sample of the stalled process shows it parked in `pthread_cond_timedwait` at about 0% CPU, which is why the job burns wall clock and not CPU.

## Fix

`later::later()` and `later::later_fd()` each return a canceller function. Keep those handles on the worker, call them when the call settles, and call them again in `worker_close()`. Note that `later::cancel()` is not exported and does not exist in later 1.4.8.

The comment above `schedule_worker_reap()` says stray timers are harmless because they check recency before acting. That holds for correctness, but not for any caller that waits on `later::loop_empty()`.

Only `MockShinySession$getOutput()` reaches `wait_for_it()`, so deployed apps do not stall. The leak itself is still real there.

title: R: an expanded definition can widen token scope for later tokens
description:
> Josh note: This issue was generated by Claude during implementation of the python data-dict definitions registry. Please feel free to close/ignore

`expand_definitions()` in `pkg-r/R/definitions.R` resolves each token against the SQL that earlier expansions have already rewritten, so a definition whose compiled SQL names another table brings that table into scope for the tokens that follow.

`resolve_definition_token()` gates a bare token on its table appearing in the query, via `definition_table_in_query()`. That check is what keeps `{{total}}` bound to the table it belongs to. Because the loop reassigns `sql` before resolving the next token, compiled SQL counts as if the author had written it.

Reproduced directly against `expand_definitions()`, with `{{sales::total}}` compiling to `sum(returns.x)` and `{{other}}` defined on `returns`:

```r
expand_definitions("SELECT {{sales::total}}, {{other}} FROM sales", defs)
#> SELECT (sum(returns.x)), (count(*)) FROM sales
```

`returns` appears nowhere in the query, so `{{other}}` should have been refused with the message that its table does not appear.

Resolving every token against the query as written, then substituting, fixes it. The Python registry now does that and refuses this input, so the two implementations disagree on which queries expand until R follows.

Two smaller differences in the same file, found alongside it:

- `definition_index_text()` caps on `cumsum(nchar(index))` but joins the kept lines with newlines, so the rendered index can exceed `cap_chars` by one character per line beyond the first. `definitions_overflow()` measures the same way.
- The missing-type case is #259.

title: R: a definition with no inferred type loses its whole gist
description:
> Josh note: This issue was generated by Claude during implementation of the python data-dict definitions registry. Please feel free to close/ignore

`definition_gist()` in `pkg-r/R/definitions.R` returns an empty string for a definition whose `type` is absent, so the definition's compiled SQL, description, and translation notes never reach the model.

data-dict omits `type` when an expression infers no single one. `survey::mixed temporal case` in the conformance corpus is such a case: a `CASE` over both a date and a datetime column. For it, `definition_gist()` returns `""`, which makes the first-touch entry and the retrieval chunk read `Governed definition {{mixed temporal case}} on table survey` and stop. The token is named but nothing says what it expands to.

The cause is `sprintf("(%s, %s)", def$kind, def$type)` with a `NULL` type. `sprintf()` returns `character(0)` for a zero-length argument, and the surrounding `paste(c(...), collapse = " ")` then collapses the rest of the gist away with it.

Found while building the Python registry, which hit the same shape. Python leaves the type out and keeps the rest, rendering `(derived) Selected SQL(duckdb): ...`, so the two implementations now differ here. Aligning them is part of the fix, and the rendered text is prompt content, which is the kind of difference that shows up as the agent behaving differently in one language rather than as an error.

title: R `check_query()` accepts writes that do not begin with a write keyword
description:
`check_query()` classifies a statement by its first word, so anything beginning with `SELECT` or `WITH` is accepted whatever follows. Six statement forms that write, lock, or create tables pass the guard.

This is a follow-up to #58. That issue reported one instance, stacked statements, and it was fixed by the semicolon check. The classification weakness #58 also described, and the parser-based fix it proposed, were not addressed, and the cases below are what remains.

[`check_query()` at `pkg-r/R/data-source.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/6937c7192aa5ee70b7f584c2886b966252398ee3/pkg-r/R/data-source.R#L719-L776) matches the denylist against the start of the normalized string, then requires the string to start with `SELECT` or `WITH`. Neither test looks past the first word.

## What is accepted

Verified against `check_query()` on `main` (R 4.6.0, DuckDB 1.5.5). All six return without error.

```
WITH t AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM sales
WITH t AS (SELECT 1) INSERT INTO sales VALUES (9)
WITH t AS (SELECT 1) UPDATE sales SET x = 5
WITH d AS (DELETE FROM sales RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM d
SELECT * INTO new_table FROM sales
SELECT * FROM sales FOR UPDATE
```

The first three are DML after a CTE list: DuckDB accepts it, and the guard sees only `WITH`. The fourth is a data-modifying CTE, where the statement reads at its root but its CTE deletes. The fifth creates a table. The sixth changes no rows but takes locks that block writers, so it is not read-only in the sense the tool advertises.

End to end through the public path, not just the guard:

```r
pkgload::load_all("pkg-r")
src <- data_source(sales = data.frame(x = 1:3))
source_query(src, "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM sales")$n
#> [1] 3
source_query(src, "WITH t AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM sales")
#> executes, with a DBI warning about dbFetch on a DELETE
source_query(src, "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM sales")$n
#> [1] 0
```

The owned DuckDB connection's `lock_down()` does not help: it disables extension loading and filesystem access, not local DML.

As in #58, this means [`read_only_hint = TRUE`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/6937c7192aa5ee70b7f584c2886b966252398ee3/pkg-r/R/tools.R#L88) and the "runs only read-only `SELECT` queries" wording currently overstate the guarantee.

## Two false rejections, from the same cause

The guard also refuses valid read-only queries, because the semicolon test runs against raw text:

```
SELECT * FROM sales WHERE note = ';'
SELECT 1 -- ; DROP TABLE sales
```

#58's suggested coverage included "do not reject keywords or semicolons inside literals, quoted identifiers, or comments". That case is still open.

## Suggested fix

Parse the statement and classify it, rather than matching its prefix. This is what #58 proposed, and the Python package has since done it in #239 using `sqlglot`: read-only statement forms are an allowlist so an unanticipated form fails closed, the whole AST is searched rather than the root so a data-modifying CTE or `SELECT INTO` cannot ride under a `SELECT`, and locking clauses are rejected.

A text-based fix is not worth attempting. The Python guard was fixed three times as a text scanner before being replaced. Skipping the CTE list with a paren scan was defeated by a `)` inside a comment, and then by DuckDB's nested block comments, because each fix needs to know one more lexical rule than the last. There is no `sqlglot` for R, so the options are DuckDB's own parser through `json_serialize_sql()` (as #58 set out in detail, though it only covers DuckDB sources) or a read-only connection where the backend supports one.

Worth deciding alongside the fix: the two packages' guards now disagree about what they accept, and the accept/reject verdicts are the kind of contract `tests/shared/` exists for. Pinning them there would keep the two from drifting further.

Filed rather than fixed alongside the Python work in #239, because this is a separate package and wants its own review.

title: How to handle data-dict's `display: restricted` column flag?
description:
data-dict's spec gives a column an optional `display` property, whose only supported value is `restricted`. It marks PII and other sensitive data. A restricted column must be excluded from default user interfaces and other user-facing output, including tables, plots, and downloads. The spec is explicit that this is a steer rather than a guarantee. See https://data-dict.tidyverse.org/spec.html#display for details.

Currently, commons doesn't do anything special with this value. The string `restricted` does not appear in `pkg-r/R`, `pkg-r/inst/prompts`, or `pkg-py/src` (verified 2026-09-01).

## Where this is relevant

`dictionary_column_line()` in `pkg-r/R/data-dictionary.R` builds a column's prompt line from its type, its description, and its examples. It does not read `display`. A restricted column is therefore described to the model exactly like every other column.

The agent gets no steer at all. It can select an SSN column and put the values in a table it shows the user, and nothing in the prompt suggests otherwise. This is the outcome the flag exists to make less likely.

## Potential implementation direction

Two places, and they are separable: mark the column in the ambient text and the first-touch entry so the model knows not to show its values by default; and respect the flag in any user-facing output commons renders itself, if it renders column values outside the model's control.

## Some other thoughts

An important note: this is more just steering for an agent and isn't really access control or a security feature (like data-dict's spec says). An agent that computes `COUNT(DISTINCT ssn)` or joins on a restricted column is doing legitimate work, and the result carries no restricted value. Refusing queries that name a restricted column would go beyond what the spec asks and would break useful analysis.

Related: data-dict's JSON export already strips `sample_values`, `common_values`, `range`, and `histogram` from a restricted column's profile and keeps only counts. Whatever commons reads from the export is already gated. The gap is the prompt text commons writes itself.

Both packages behave the same way today, so an eventual answer definition belongs in `tests/shared/` and implemented on both sides.

title: Audit trail silently drops conversations/branches: conversation_id never rotates across shinychat history operations
description:
## Problem

`Commons` mints `private$conversation_id` exactly once, in `initialize()`, and nothing ever rotates it. But shinychat's history controller reuses **one client object for every logical conversation in a session**:

- **New chat** (`HistoryController$new_chat`): `client$set_turns(list())` — same client.
- **Conversation switching** (`switch_to`): `set_turns()` to a completely different stored conversation — same client.
- **Edit** (`handle_edit`): truncates turns to the fork parent via `set_turns()`, then resubmits.
- **Branch navigation** (`handle_navigate`): `set_turns()` to a different leaf of the message tree.

So in the trace, every conversation a user touches in one Shiny session is recorded under a single `commons.conversation.id`.

## Impact: exchanges silently vanish from the audit trail

`build_trajectories()` keeps only the **latest chat span per conversation id** as the canonical history. Two consequences:

1. **New chat / switch:** a user has a 5-exchange conversation, clicks "New chat", asks one question. The latest chat span under the shared id carries only the new conversation's turns — the first conversation's five exchanges disappear from `trajectory_read()` entirely.
2. **Edits / branch navigation:** after an edit-and-regenerate (or navigating back to an earlier sibling and continuing), only the final active path survives review. Answers the user actually saw — rendered with a trust verdict — become unreviewable.

For a governance/audit tool this is the worst kind of gap: it's silent. The reviewer has no signal that anything is missing.

Note the exchange-provenance matching added in the server-side citation verification work already anticipates the id-sharing (see "switched conversations do not donate audit records" and "edited paths retain shared-prefix records and drop abandoned records" in `test-trajectories.R`) — records are correctly never cross-contaminated between logical conversations. That defends the *records*; the *turn content* still evaporates via latest-span-wins.

## Recommended fix

**Rotate `conversation_id` whenever history diverges.** Have `Commons` override `set_turns()` (or detect at `stream_async()` time) that the current turns are not an extension of the last-streamed state, and mint a new id.

Because every chat span carries its full history prefix, the new id's spans still carry the restored/forked history — nothing is lost, and `latest_chat_spans()` stops collapsing distinct conversations.

Trade-off: one logical conversation restored across sessions appears under multiple ids, so review shows some duplicated prefix history. Duplication beats disappearance for an audit tool, and the prefix-comparison machinery in `trajectory-read.R` could dedupe later.

### Alternative / complement

`build_trajectories()` already parses every recorded call's chat span (post citation-verification branch). It could detect that some spans are *not* prefixes of the latest one — i.e., abandoned branches or displaced conversations — and surface them, even just as "N branches/conversations not shown", closing the silent part of the gap without a UI redesign.

## Related

- Mid-stream mutation race (smaller, separate): shinychat's `handle_edit`/`new_chat`/`switch_to` observers are not gated on stream status, so turns can be mutated between `stream_async()`'s `from_index` capture and its completion-time `self$get_turns()` read, recording a tag computed from unrelated turns. Deriving tags from content that flowed through the stream itself would remove the race.

*(Observed against shinychat 0.4.0.9000.)*

The package's system requirements resolve to chromium, so pak's `pre_install` runs `add-apt-repository -y ppa:xtradeb/apps`. That fetches the PPA signing key from Launchpad, and when Launchpad's API returns HTTP 500 the step dies with `GPGKeyTemporarilyNotFoundError`.

Because the three workflows share the step, one Launchpad hiccup fails all three at once, in about 90 seconds. The jobs look like a code failure but nothing was compiled or tested.

Seen on #163 (2026-08-25): all three failed, two passed on retry, `pkgdown` then failed the same way on two further retries.

Worth considering: install chromium without the PPA, ship or pin the signing key, or retry the sysreqs step. Whichever way, the goal is that a Launchpad outage stops blocking every PR that touches `pkg-r/` or `tests/shared/`.
