title: Per-viewer access to data and facts
description:
commons agents are built by data scientists who have access to different information than the intended users of the app.

For agents scoped to smaller domains, this isn't as much of an issue; only those who have access to the underlying data should be given access to the app.

For more general data agents, the question is trickier. What happens when the CEO looks at the app vs. a product owner multiple levels down?

There are two axes in question here:

* **Row-level access** is more important and should be more straightforward, at least for Snowflake and Databricks. Run every query as the viewer via connect's viewer-based credentials. Document `data_source(DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake()), ...)` inside `server()` as the happy path (explaining that connectcreds/odbc will do the heavy lifting here). Elsewhere—Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server—the story is trickier. pins would be per-pin via a visitor API key and need per-session board auth (today the board source downloads is process-wide).
* **Fact-level access** is less important and more tricky. In `data_source(con, data_dictionary)`, the machine-readability of data dictionaries should be helpful for us in that only the tables from `con` that the user has access to should be searchable by the model.`context_layer()` is harder. 

There should probably be GRC-focused vignette that, among other things, makes it clear we're not putting any trust in the LLM itself to not leak information.

<details>
<summary>Initial prompt to Fable</summary>

> Up to this point, I've largely tabled the GRC question with commons. Notably, commons agents are built by data scientists who might have access to different information than the users of the app. To some extent, this can be solved by only allowing access to the application to certain people inside of Connect; this works already. That said, We imagine that some folks will take this agent and make it relatively general, like a "Data at \[company\] agent". This means that the privacy story might be rather tricky, e.g. what happens when the CEO looks at the app vs. a product owner 3 levels down?
> 
> There are at least two big questions here:
> 
> * Row-level access permissions on the data itself. For data that's inside of Snowflake or Databricks or whatever, I think this should actually be relatively easy? We probably don't need a story for data that is inside of playing tables, for example.
> * Fact-level access permissions. e.g. should anyone with access to the app have access to any of the information in the data dictionary or context layer?
> 
> Via Connect, we have access to some bits of information about who it is that is looking at the app at a given moment. You have access to the Connect source code--feel free to clone it into inst/ and read the relevant pieces. You also have access to a Connect API, so feel free to experiment against the live service. https://github.com/posit-dev/connectcreds might also be useful.
> 
> The work in this PR might be relevant: https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/48, https://github.com/tidyverse/data-dict/issues/134, https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/issues/40
> 
> Explore thoroughly and put yourself in the shoes of the data scientist who wants to adopt commons, and the stakeholders that data scientist will need to convince that it's okay. At the same time, consider the difficulty (or maybe ease) of fact-level access permissions.
> 
> Write a thorough report on GRC with commons deployed on Connect within organizations. Consider the various use cases of commons (relatively small, domain-specific app vs. 'Data at \[Company\]' app) and the various data environments it might need to hook up to (Databricks, Snowflake, other SQL databases, Connect pins, local tables). How can we make sure users of commons apps only have access to the information they should without introducing unnecessary burden for the maintainer of the commons app? Write clearly.

</details>


<details>
<summary>Write-up from Fable</summary>

> # GRC for commons agents deployed on Posit Connect
> 
> Date: 2026-07-27
> 
> The question: commons agents are built by data scientists who may have access to
> different information than the app's users. When the app is small and
> domain-specific, Connect's content access controls mostly settle the matter. When
> the app grows toward "Data at [Company]" — one agent, many audiences, the CEO and
> a product owner three levels down looking at the same URL — two harder questions
> appear:
> 
> 1. **Row-level access to the data itself.** Can the agent's queries run with the
>    viewer's data permissions rather than the publisher's?
> 2. **Fact-level access to the harness.** Should every viewer see every dictionary
>    entry, metric definition, and context-layer document?
> 
> This report maps what Connect provides today (verified against Connect's
> behavior and docs, and against the live connect.posit.it server), what commons
> does today, where the two meet, and what commons should build. The short version:
> 
> - Row-level access is indeed **largely a solved problem for Snowflake, Databricks,
>   BigQuery, and Azure-token-capable databases**, via Connect's viewer OAuth
>   integrations — provided commons apps construct their data sources per Shiny
>   session. The warehouse stays the single source of truth; commons inherits
>   row-level security, column masking, and object grants for free.
> - Fact-level access has one honest cheap answer (scope the app's audience; deploy
>   per-audience variants) and one good derived answer (**let data access imply fact
>   access**: subset the dictionary/pool to tables the viewer's connection can
>   actually query). Hand-maintained per-fact ACLs should be a last resort.
> - The sharpest current edge isn't either of those: it's that **the boundary of
>   `run_sql` is the connection's privileges, not the registered table list**, plus
>   a handful of process-model footguns (shared agents, shared in-process caches)
>   that commons should close before any of this matters.
> 
> Throughout, "the harness" means everything commons assembles for the model:
> system prompt, dictionary content, glossary, measures/definitions/metrics pool,
> context layer, and tool set.
> 
> ## 1. The one principle everything else follows from
> 
> **Anything that enters the harness is disclosed to every user who can open the
> app.** A viewer with enough patience can extract the system prompt, the
> dictionary prose, every measure description, and anything `search_context` can
> retrieve. Instructing the model to withhold information from certain users is not
> a control; no security reviewer will accept it, and they'll be right.
> 
> So both questions above reduce to the same architectural statement: *permissions
> must be enforced when the harness and its connections are assembled — per
> session, before the model runs — or one layer down, in systems (warehouse,
> Connect) that enforce them regardless of what the model does.* Everything below
> is about where that assembly-time enforcement can live and what it costs the
> maintainer.
> 
> ## 2. What Connect provides
> 
> Verified against Connect's behavior and docs, and live against connect.posit.it.
> 
> ### 2.1 Who can open the app
> 
> Content access types: all, logged-in, or an ACL of named users and groups.
> Groups can be provisioned from LDAP/OIDC (connect.posit.it has 657 of them,
> mostly IdP-synced). This is coarse (whole app), robust, and already understood by
> IT. For the domain-specific archetype it is the entire story.
> 
> ### 2.2 Who is looking, from inside the app
> 
> Connect's proxy injects a credentials header into every proxied request; Shiny
> surfaces it as `session$user` and `session$groups`. Two properties matter:
> 
> - It's trustworthy: the proxy strips any forged credential headers on incoming
>   requests before injecting its own.
> - Its *format* is configurable and org-dependent: values are usernames/group
>   names by default, but `Authorization.ContentCredentialsUseGUID`/`UseDN` switch
>   them to GUIDs or LDAP DNs, and Connect's own docs warn names may not be unique
>   in large orgs. Anything keying on `session$groups` needs to treat the values
>   as opaque, org-configured identifiers.
> 
> Anonymous viewers (access type "all") have no identity; every per-viewer
> mechanism below requires logged-in viewers.
> 
> ### 2.3 Acting *as* the viewer: the credential exchange
> 
> This is the load-bearing primitive. Connect attaches a short-lived JWT (24h,
> job-scoped, viewer-GUID subject) to every interactive request as the
> `Posit-Connect-User-Session-Token` header. Content POSTs it to
> `/v1/oauth/integrations/credentials` (RFC 8693 token exchange) and receives, per
> the integration configured by an administrator:
> 
> | Integration | Auth types | What content receives |
> |---|---|---|
> | Snowflake | Viewer only | Viewer's Snowflake OAuth access token |
> | Databricks | Viewer, Service Account, Workload Identity | Viewer's (or service) Databricks token |
> | BigQuery / Google Cloud, Azure (Entra), AWS | Viewer and/or service | Viewer's cloud token / AWS credentials |
> | Connect API | Visitor API Key | **Ephemeral Connect API key acting as the viewer**, capped by `max_role`, deleted when the content process exits |
> | Custom / Vault / OIDC federation | varies | Arbitrary OAuth-fronted services, per-workload secrets |
> 
> Operational properties worth quoting to a security reviewer: the admin creates
> integrations centrally ("acquire and reuse the organization's existing data
> access policies from a single centralized location"); the publisher associates an
> integration with a content item; the viewer authorizes once and Connect stores
> and refreshes their tokens encrypted server-side; refresh tokens never reach the
> content; exchanges are audit-logged; the subject token only works from the
> content process the viewer actually visited.
> 
> The R ergonomics are already excellent: `connectcreds::connect_viewer_token()`
> does the exchange with per-session caching, and — decisive for commons —
> **`odbc::snowflake()` and `odbc::databricks()` call it automatically** when
> running in a Shiny session on Connect. A publisher writes:
> 
> ```r
> server <- function(input, output, session) {
>   con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake())   # viewer's identity, automatically
>   ...
> }
> ```
> 
> connect.posit.it already has the relevant integrations live: a Snowflake viewer
> integration, three Connect API visitor-key integrations, and service-account
> integrations — so all of this is testable today on the server the demo deploys
> to.
> 
> ### 2.4 What Connect records
> 
> - Connect logs content visits (who, when) independently of the app.
> - commons' `log = TRUE` trajectories land in Connect's observability store,
>   readable by the content owner and collaborators — i.e., editor access, and
>   only for publisher-and-up accounts (commons' `share_with` docs already say
>   this). Viewer-role accounts cannot read traces.
> - Because trajectories land in Connect's store, their retention, redaction, and
>   export are administered at the Connect level rather than by commons. commons'
>   trajectory story should ride whatever controls the platform exposes over
>   prompts and responses, not build a parallel scheme.
> 
> ### 2.5 What Connect does *not* provide
> 
> - No per-viewer environment variables or secrets. In fact the opposite: by
>   default (`Applications.DefaultAPIKeyEnv = true`), every content process gets an
>   ephemeral `CONNECT_API_KEY` **that acts as the content owner** — the publisher.
>   The app process is a confused-deputy risk by construction; more in §6.
> - No row-level enforcement for databases without token-based auth (Postgres,
>   MySQL, on-prem SQL Server). Legacy escape hatches exist (PAM "run as current
>   user" with Kerberos delegation for Shiny), but they're niche.
> - No fact-level anything: Connect governs content items and data credentials, not
>   fragments of an app's prompt.
> 
> ## 3. Where the boundaries actually are in a commons app
> 
> Four nested boundaries, from outside in:
> 
> **B0 — the app.** Connect ACL. Who can converse with the agent at all.
> 
> **B1 — the connection.** What the agent's SQL can physically read. A critical
> observation about commons today: `run_sql` applies a write-keyword denylist and
> nothing else — *it does not restrict queries to registered tables*. The `tables=`
> registry drives documentation, first-touch, and `describe_table`, but a model
> (or a viewer who asks nicely) can `SELECT` from any table the connection can
> reach. That's fine — a table allowlist parsed from SQL would be a false comfort
> anyway (views, functions, `information_schema` reach) — but it means **the honest
> statement of the data boundary is: "the agent can read whatever its DBI
> connection can read."** Stakeholder conversations should be had in exactly those
> terms, and the mitigation is credential scoping (a service account granted only
> the intended schema, or viewer credentials), never SQL inspection.
> 
> **B2 — the harness.** What the model has been told: dictionary, glossary,
> metrics/definitions, context layer, measure descriptions. Today assembled once,
> identically for everyone.
> 
> **B3 — the record.** Trajectories, traces, eval sets, critique queues. Contains
> both user questions and query *results* (tool outputs ride in spans when content
> capture is on).
> 
> Row-level access is a B1 problem. Fact-level access is a B2 problem. A lot of
> GRC review pain is B3. The next three sections take them in turn.
> 
> ## 4. Row-level access, by data environment
> 
> ### Snowflake, Databricks (and BigQuery, Azure-token databases)
> 
> Use viewer OAuth integrations; run every query as the viewer. The warehouse's own
> row access policies, column masks, and object grants then govern — the same
> enforcement the org already trusts for every other tool, applied to the person
> asking, not the person who built the app. This is also exactly the pattern the
> vendor agents use (Databricks Genie answers "with the asking user's Unity Catalog
> permissions"; Snowflake semantic views enforce the querying role's privileges),
> so it's a story security teams have already accepted once.
> 
> What it takes in a commons app, given odbc's connectcreds support:
> 
> ```r
> server <- function(input, output, session) {
>   agent <- commons(
>     chat_anthropic(),
>     data_sources = data_source(
>       DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake()),      # viewer-scoped
>       tables = c("sales.orders", "sales.accounts"),
>       dictionary = "sales.data-dict.yaml"
>     ),
>     context_layer = context_layer(files = "notes.md")
>   )
>   commons_server("chat", agent)
> }
> ```
> 
> The design consequence: **the data source, and therefore the agent, must be
> constructed inside the session**, not at the top of `app.R`. commons' docs
> already say "Create a new agent for each Shiny session," but nothing enforces or
> eases it (see §7). Per-session construction currently pays for table probes, a
> dictionary parse, and (lazily) a context index per session — cheap enough for a
> first version, worth a template/bind split later.
> 
> Residual considerations, all manageable:
> 
> - Startup latency: one OAuth exchange (cached per session) plus a warehouse
>   connection per session.
> - Token lifetime: Connect refreshes on every exchange; an open ODBC connection
>   outliving its token is a reconnect concern, not a security one.
> - A viewer whose grants don't cover a registered table sees errors from the
>   warehouse. Better: probe and subset at session start — which is the bridge to
>   fact-level access (§5).
> - Measures/definitions that take the source's connection inherit viewer scoping
>   automatically — a nice existing property of commons' design (governed
>   computations run *as the viewer* with zero extra work). Measures that embed
>   their own credentials (a `board =` default argument, an API client) do not,
>   and remain publisher-scoped; worth a documentation callout.
> 
> ### Other SQL databases (Postgres, MySQL, on-prem SQL Server)
> 
> No viewer-token path in general. Realistic options, in order:
> 
> 1. **Accept app-identity access and control at B0.** Create a database role
>    scoped to exactly the tables the app should expose, read-only; state plainly
>    that everyone admitted to the app shares that access. For most domain apps
>    this is the right answer, and it's the same answer a dashboard over the same
>    data would give.
> 2. Azure SQL / cloud-hosted engines that accept AAD/IAM tokens: the Azure/AWS
>    viewer integrations make these behave like the warehouse case.
> 3. Kerberos + PAM run-as-current-user (Shiny only, on-prem only): real but
>    legacy; don't build for it.
> 
> Do **not** offer app-layer row filtering ("append `WHERE region = viewer's
> region`" to model SQL) as a security feature. Templated views created outside the
> model's control could make it *correct*, but the connection can still read the
> unfiltered table (B1), so it's UX, not enforcement. If a design ever adds this,
> it must be named a convenience filter, never RLS.
> 
> ### Connect pins
> 
> Pins have real ACLs on Connect, and the Visitor API Key integration lets the app
> read them *as the viewer*: exchange the session token for an ephemeral key, then
> `board_connect(auth = "manual", key = <ephemeral>)`. Access is per-pin
> (all-or-nothing), not per-row — but per-pin is exactly the granularity pins users
> already manage.
> 
> commons' current board source works against this: pins are downloaded once into
> a process-wide DuckDB (with a startup prewarm) using whatever credentials the
> *process* holds, and every session served by that process reads the same tables.
> Viewer-scoped boards require: per-session board auth, per-viewer (or no)
> caching, and accepting that the prewarm optimization only applies to
> publisher-scoped boards. This is a real but well-contained architecture change
> (§7).
> 
> ### Local tables (data frames baked into the deployment)
> 
> No per-viewer story is possible: the data ships inside the bundle and lives in a
> process-shared DuckDB. That's not a gap to fix; it's a property to document.
> **If data is loaded into the app, B0 is the only boundary** — the app's audience
> is the data's audience. The maintainer guidance writes itself: data with
> differentiated access belongs behind a connection that can enforce the
> difference, not in the bundle.
> 
> One subtlety worth closing regardless: the in-process DuckDB (frames and boards
> alike) is shared across all Shiny sessions on a process, and Connect runs
> multiple sessions per process and multiple processes per content item. Nothing
> sensitive crosses *content* items, but publishers should understand that "my
> session's tables" are actually "this process's tables."
> 
> ## 5. Fact-level access
> 
> What counts as a fact here: a dictionary table entry, a glossary term, a metric
> or definition (`expr` + description), a verified query, a context-layer document,
> a measure's description. Every one of them reaches the model, so every one is
> B2 — assembly-time — material.
> 
> ### The honest default: the app is the unit of disclosure
> 
> For the domain-specific archetype, don't build fact-level permissions. State the
> posture: *everything this app knows, every user of this app may learn.* Scope B0
> accordingly. This is auditable in one sentence and it's how every dashboard the
> org already runs works. commons' documentation should say this explicitly, and
> mean it.
> 
> The same posture scales further than it first appears via **per-audience
> deployments**: the "Data at [Company]" app can be a *family* of deployments of
> one parameterized harness — same code, different `data_source()`s / context
> files per audience, each content item ACL'd to its group. This has a GRC
> property no dynamic scheme matches: the reviewable artifact is static. An
> auditor can open the exec variant and the org-wide variant and diff what each
> knows. Costs: N deployments to keep updated (automatable; it's one `deployApp()`
> loop), and coarse granularity (audience-level, not user-level).
> 
> ### The derived answer: data access implies fact access
> 
> When sources are viewer-scoped (§4), fact-level visibility can be *derived*
> instead of authored. At session start, commons already probes registered tables
> with zero-row `SELECT`s (`check_table_ids_exist()`); with a viewer connection,
> a failed probe means *this viewer can't read this table* — so drop, for this
> session: the table from the registry, its dictionary entry, its definitions and
> metrics from the pool, its dictionary-derived context chunks, and its mention in
> the prompt.
> 
> This is the design worth being proudest of, because it has the property GRC
> people actually want: **no second source of truth.** The warehouse grant is the
> policy; the harness conforms to it automatically; revoking a grant revokes the
> facts at the next session. Fail-closed (no grant, no probe success, no fact),
> zero per-fact maintenance, and it directly answers "what happens when the CEO
> looks at the app vs. the product owner" — they get different harnesses derived
> from their different grants.
> 
> Limits to state clearly:
> 
> - Granularity is the table (or whatever object the warehouse secures). Fine in
>   practice: dictionaries, definitions, and metrics are already table-scoped in
>   both commons and the data-dict spec sketch (#134).
> - Free-text context files aren't table-attributed. Options: attribute them
>   (frontmatter `tables:` — `context_layer()` already parses and strips
>   frontmatter), or leave free context always-visible and say so.
> - Column masking is invisible to probes; a masked column's dictionary entry
>   would still show. Acceptable — the *definition* of a masked column is usually
>   not the secret — but worth a sentence in docs.
> 
> ### The authored answer: audience tags
> 
> Where facts must diverge from data grants (or sources aren't viewer-scoped), the
> remaining option is explicit audience metadata keyed to Connect groups, checked
> against `session$groups` at assembly:
> 
> ```r
> data_source(con, dictionary = "finance.yaml", audience = "finance-leadership")
> context_layer(files = c("public-notes.md", "board-prep.md"))
> # board-prep.md frontmatter:  audience: [executive-team]
> ```
> 
> Precedent exists for pushing this into the dictionary itself — Snowflake
> semantic views mark facts `PRIVATE`; data-dict already has `display: restricted`
> for PII — so an `audience:`/`visibility:` field on tables and definitions is a
> plausible data-dict #134-adjacent conversation. But be sober about the costs
> before recommending it widely:
> 
> - It's a second permission system, hand-maintained, keyed on group identifiers
>   whose format is org-configurable (names vs. GUIDs vs. DNs) and whose
>   membership commons can't see beyond the header.
> - Silent drift is the failure mode: warehouse says yes, tag says no (harmless),
>   or tag says yes to a group whose meaning changed (leak).
> - Fact-level restriction without matching data-level restriction protects only
>   the *documentation*: if the connection can read the table, `run_sql` can
>   query it whether or not the harness mentions it, and aggregate questions can
>   reconstruct facts ("what's the average salary of the two people on team X?").
>   Tags must therefore always pair with B1 scoping for the same subject — the
>   docs should refuse to present tags as standalone confidentiality.
> 
> Recommended ordering when a maintainer asks: B0 audience scoping → per-audience
> deployments → derived visibility → audience tags, stopping at the first level
> that satisfies the requirement. Most apps should stop at the first or second.
> 
> ### Sensitive values inside the harness itself
> 
> Independent of viewers: dictionaries carry `examples`/`values`, context files
> carry quotes, and `describe_table` samples five live rows into the conversation
> (and thus into traces and the LLM provider's context). For a table of, say, HR
> records, the *sample* is the leak. Worth a `sample_rows = 0` style option on
> `data_source()` and a dictionary-respecting default (data-dict's
> `display: restricted` should suppress example values in prompts). Small change,
> disproportionate GRC value.
> 
> ## 6. The record, and the process
> 
> The B3 material a reviewer will ask about, and current answers:
> 
> - **What does the LLM provider see?** Questions, harness content, query results
>   (rows), and R tool outputs. Answer: the org chooses the provider (`client=`),
>   including self-hosted; this is the same disclosure surface as any LLM app the
>   org runs, and commons adds no additional exfiltration channel (run_sql is
>   read-only; run_r is sandboxed and network-restricted).
> - **Who can read trajectories?** Owner + collaborators with publisher-level
>   accounts, via editor-gated trace APIs; `share_with` grants deliberately.
>   User questions are personal data once viewer identity is attached — which it
>   currently is not: commons spans carry a conversation id but *no viewer
>   identity*. That's simultaneously an audit gap (can't answer "who asked this")
>   and a privacy default (no per-user question dossiers). Decide on purpose;
>   don't leave it accidental. Recommendation: record `session$user` as a span
>   attribute, off by default, one argument to turn on — and document retention
>   as Connect-governed.
> - **Redaction and retention:** trajectories live in Connect's observability
>   store, so "can we turn conversation retention off org-wide" is a question for
>   Connect administrators, not for commons. `log = TRUE` docs should point at the
>   platform's controls rather than reimplement them.
> - **The process itself:** the content process holds publisher-grade credentials
>   — `CONNECT_API_KEY` (owner-scoped, injected by default), LLM keys, any service
>   DB creds. commons already does the right things where the model touches the
>   process: `run_r` workers start from a scrubbed env allowlist and an OS sandbox
>   (Seatbelt/Landlock), and `run_sql` blocks writes with DuckDB locked down for
>   owned connections. The remaining exposures are conventional app-security ones
>   (the publisher's own code, `envVars` hygiene, admins optionally disabling
>   `DefaultAPIKeyEnv`), and one commons-specific one:
> - **The shared-agent footgun.** `commons()` at the top of `app.R` shares one
>   Chat object — *including turn history* — across every concurrent session in a
>   process, and shinychat does not clone the client, so two simultaneous users
>   would interleave conversations. This has nothing to do with permissions design
>   and should be closed first.
> - **Context supply chain.** Whoever can edit a context file or dictionary
>   steers the agent (including "cite this authoritative-sounding claim").
>   Fact-level *write* governance is just git review on those files; the
>   provenance pills (A/B/C) are the runtime mitigation and already exist. Worth
>   one paragraph in a governance vignette, not new machinery.
> 
> ## 7. What commons should build
> 
> Ordered by leverage; the first two are prerequisites for any of the rest being
> meaningful.
> 
> 1. **Close the shared-agent hazard.** `commons_server()` can detect that the
>    same `Commons` object is bound in two live sessions (or simply clone with a
>    warning). Also audit the example apps to construct per-session. Small.
> 2. **Make per-session, viewer-scoped construction the documented happy path.**
>    A vignette section showing `data_source(DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake()),
>    ...)` inside `server()`, with the connectcreds/odbc behavior explained, plus
>    a `commons_server()` variant accepting a factory (`function(session)
>    commons(...)`) so the pattern is hard to get wrong. Small–medium.
> 3. **`sample_rows` control + `display: restricted` respect** in prompts and
>    `describe_table`. Small.
> 4. **Viewer identity in trajectories, opt-in** (`log_viewer = TRUE` recording
>    `session$user`/GUID on the conversation's spans). Small.
> 5. **Derived visibility for viewer-scoped sources.** Reuse the existing probe
>    machinery per session; filter registry, dictionary delivery, pool entries,
>    and dictionary-derived context chunks by probe results. Medium; highest
>    fact-level payoff per unit of new concept.
> 6. **Template/bind split** so per-session assembly is cheap: parse dictionary,
>    read context files, and build indexes once; bind `con` + viewer filter per
>    session. Medium, driven by whatever latency #2 and #5 measure.
> 7. **Viewer-scoped board sources** (visitor API key + per-viewer/no cache).
>    Medium; do when a real adopter needs governed pins.
> 8. **Audience tags** on sources and context files (and the data-dict `audience:`
>    conversation alongside #134). Do last, deliberately, with docs that pair
>    them with B1 scoping.
> 9. **A governance vignette** — essentially §§3–6 of this report from the
>    adopting data scientist's point of view: the one-pager they hand their
>    security review. Cheap and probably the highest-adoption-leverage item here.
> 
> ## 8. The stakeholder pitch, compressed
> 
> What a data scientist can honestly tell their security team about a well-built
> commons app on Connect:
> 
> > Access to the app is governed by our IdP groups through Connect. Every query
> > the agent runs is read-only and executes against [Snowflake] *as the person
> > asking*, so row-level security and masking apply exactly as they do in every
> > other tool; the app holds no warehouse credentials of its own for user
> > queries. The agent's knowledge (definitions, documentation) is
> > [visible to all users of this app / derived per-user from warehouse grants].
> > Agent-generated code runs in an OS-sandboxed worker with no credentials or
> > network. Conversations [are / are not] logged; logs live in Connect, readable
> > only by the app's maintainers and subject to our Connect administrators'
> > policy. Answers from governed definitions are labeled; everything else is
> > visibly marked as unverified.
> 
> Every clause in that paragraph is backed by a mechanism in this report — and the
> clauses commons can't yet back ("derived per-user", the factory pattern, viewer
> attribution) are the work list in §7.
> 
> ## File references
> 
> - commons: `R/connect.R`, `R/data-source.R` (`check_query()` at ~479,
>   `check_table_ids_exist()` at ~658, `duckdb_lock_down()`), `R/chat.R`
>   (`commons_server()`), `R/run-r.R` (`worker_scrubbed_env()` at ~276),
>   `R/tools.R` (`tool_run_sql()`), `R/context-layer.R`, PR #48 branch
>   `origin/definitions-6` (`R/pool.R`, `R/definitions.R`)

title: A higher-level pass through docs
description:
The documentation is currently pretty feature-by-feature. There are a few higher-level points worth making prominently, maybe with figures or diagrams:

## commons does 3 things

1) Helps data scientists extract and format various kinds of agent context
2) Makes that context available to agents via a scaffold
3) Provides tooling to help data scientists monitor the agent and improve 1) based on interactions with the deployed agent

## There are 2 paths

1) Semantic layer
2) Hand-authored SQL

## The scaffold has $n$ tools and a prompt

Outline the 5 (currently) tools and document how different pieces of the context—data dictionaries, measures definitions, "loose" context—get injected at different moments.

(Should those tools / prompt be made available via an MCP server?)

title: Should `context_layer()` be a thing at all?
description: Should it all live in the data dictionary, regardless of where the measures live? Or is genuinely free-form, add-whatever-in-whatever-unstructured-format still useful?

title: `data-dict.yaml` as an interoperable semantic layer format
description:
Spent some time this afternoon prodding at the commons/querychat/canvas interoperability story, where data-dict.yaml becomes a standard format that any of the tools could read from. * @hadley is open to the semantic layer being defined / documented in `data-dict.yaml`. * The major vendors support grabbing the relevant stuff with a query. - Snowflake is `SYSTEM$READ_YAML_FROM_SEMANTIC_VIEW('db.schema.view')` returns the entire definition as YAML in one SQL call - Databricks is `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED catalog.schema.my_metric_view AS JSON` gives the Unity Catalog basics, with additional Genie-specific commands later - dbt is `SELECT * FROM {{ semantic_layer.metrics() }}`, also yaml * The major vendors (and Apache Ossie, a spec adopted by the above two plus dbt) need a few additions to the current spec: - `metrics` (per-table): named aggregate SQL expressions with a description, e.g. `expr: SUM(order_total * (1 - discount))`. Snowflake calls these `METRICS` in a semantic view; Databricks calls them `measures` in a metric view. - `queries`: vetted SQL statements with optional typed parameters (parameter descriptors can reuse the existing column grammar: `type`, `values`, `range`). Snowflake calls these verified queries (`AI_VERIFIED_QUERIES`); Databricks Genie calls them trusted assets (parameterized example queries and SQL table functions). - `filters`: named boolean expressions defining reusable segments, e.g. `expr: region IN ('US', 'CA', 'MX')`. Snowflake marks these with `LABELS = (FILTER)` on a dimension (named `filters` in the legacy YAML); Databricks has a metric-view-level `filter` and "filter" SQL expressions in Genie. So, something like: ```yaml $version: 0.2.0 name: sales tables: - name: orders description: One row per completed order since 2020. source: sql: sales.orders # already planned for the spec columns: - name: order_total type: number(quantity) units: USD range: [0, .inf] - name: region type: enum values: [AMER, EMEA, APAC] - name: status_cd type: enum values: {90: realized, 10: pending, 20: cancelled} metrics: # NEW: governed aggregations - name: net_revenue label: Net revenue description: Realized revenue net of discounts. Only status 90 counts. expr: SUM(order_total * adj_fctr) FILTER (WHERE status_cd = 90) origin: # optional pointer to the system of record snowflake_semantic_view: SALES_DB.PUBLIC.SALES_METRICS metric: NET_REVENUE filters: # NEW: named segments - name: enterprise description: Mid-Market-3 through Enterprise-3 accounts. expr: tile_size IN ('Mid-Market-3', 'Enterprise-1', 'Enterprise-2', 'Enterprise-3') queries: # NEW: verified, parameterized queries - name: open_opps_in_region description: Open opportunities in the given regions. parameters: - name: regions type: enum values: [AMER, EMEA, APAC] sql: | SELECT * FROM opportunities WHERE status = 'open' AND region IN ({regions}) verified_by: jane verified_at: 2026-07-01 ``` commons could then read this in fine. (measures would probably be renamed to metrics.) We would keep the existing measureroxygen2-style markup so that R functions can also be measures. In the current interface, this would flow through `data_source()` rather than `semantic_layer()`. A bit awkward, so worth reconsidering. The first step would probably be a subcommand family in `data-dict` that converts Snowflake and Databricks semantic layers into `data-dict`s.
A more complete write-up from Fable:

> # Semantic layer interoperability: commons, querychat, data-dict, Snowflake, Databricks > > Date: 2026-07-22 > > Prompted by a conversation with Hadley: commons and data-dict can share work on > "converting snowflake/databricks semantic definitions," and data-dict.yaml's scope may be > broader than its site currently conveys. The framing questions for this report: > > 1. How should commons support Snowflake and Databricks semantic layers? > 2. What can commons, querychat, and other downstream apps inherit from data-dict.yaml — > in particular, could data-dict.yaml be the first-class place where the semantic layer > (commons' measures) lives, such that commons adopts them right out of the dictionary? > > ## Summary > > The vendor semantic formats have converged on a small, stable core: tables bound to > physical sources, columns/dimensions with `name`/`expr`/`description`/`synonyms`, > aggregate measures with `name`/`expr`/`description`/`synonyms`, key-based relationships > with cardinality, and NL affordances (sample values, verified queries, freeform AI > instructions). data-dict.yaml already covers the *descriptive* half of that core — often > with more rigor than the vendors (constraints, ranges, units, time zones, PII flags, > validation against data). What it lacks is the *query* half: metrics, named filters, > synonyms, and verified/parameterized queries. > > Given that Hadley is open to expanding data-dict's definition, the recommendation is: > > - Extend data-dict.yaml with a small query-semantics vocabulary: per-table `metrics` > (declarative aggregate expressions), per-column `synonyms`, top-level named `filters` > (segments), and top-level `queries` (verified, optionally parameterized SQL). This is > deliberately the convergent vendor core, so Snowflake semantic views and Databricks > metric views convert into it nearly mechanically — and it is exactly the set commons > needs to derive a semantic layer directly from the dictionary. > - commons then treats the dictionary as the first-class authoring surface: tools > compiled from dictionary `metrics`/`queries` become tag-A tools, with R functions > remaining the escape hatch for computation SQL can't express. commons is pre-release > and will rename its own vocabulary (`measure()`, and "measure" throughout) to match > whatever the spec settles on. > - Both extraction directions are practical today: Snowflake exports a complete semantic > view as YAML in one SQL call; Databricks exposes metric-view YAML via `DESCRIBE`, UC > comments/keys via information_schema, and (with caveats) full Genie curation via one > REST GET. A `data-dict harvest`-style converter is the shared work between the > projects. > - Watch Apache Ossie (the Open Semantic Interchange spec, formerly OSI) rather than > target it yet; align new field names with it where free. > > ## 1. Where each tool stands today > > ### commons > > commons already has both layers of the eventual architecture, but the semantic layer is > narrow ("currently just a set of measures" — issue #6): > > - `data_source(dictionary=)` consumes data-dict.yaml. Dataset prose and glossary go in > the system prompt; a table's full entry is delivered on first touch (via > `describe_table` or `run_sql`); dictionary prose is indexed into the context layer > (`R/data-dictionary.R`, `R/context-layer.R`). > - `semantic_layer()` is a registry of `measure()`s: name, description, typed > model-visible arguments (ellmer types), and an executable R body with data source > connections injected (`R/measures.R`, `R/read-measures.R`). Answers route through > `search_measures` → `call_measure` first; SQL is the marked-lower-trust fallback > (tags A and B). > - `inst/references/semantic-layer-landscape.md` already sketches the broadened object > model (dimensions, segments, entities, provenance, adapters like > `databricks_metric_views(con)`), and `inst/references/context-semantic-graph-layers.md` > maps the vendor landscape. This report is largely about *where those objects should be > authored* — and the answer proposed here is: in the data dictionary. > > ### querychat > > querychat (posit-dev, R + Python) is the closest prior art for both integrations: > > - `data_dict` argument: a data-dict.yaml is read and rendered into the system prompt > (table descriptions, relationships, glossary; column detail stripped) — > `pkg-r/R/DataDict.R`. > - Snowflake semantic views: on a Snowflake connection it runs `SHOW SEMANTIC VIEWS`, > fetches each DDL via `GET_DDL('SEMANTIC_VIEW', ...)`, and inlines the raw DDL into the > system prompt along with `SEMANTIC_VIEW()` query syntax guidance and an instruction to > prefer semantic views over raw tables (`pkg-r/R/DBISource.R`, > `inst/prompts/semantic-views/`). Python mirrors this (`_snowflake.py`). > - No Databricks-specific support yet. > > querychat's approach is "dump the vendor definition into the prompt and teach the model > the query syntax." It works, but the definition isn't normalized: nothing downstream can > enumerate the metrics, type their parameters, build UI from them, or share them with a > non-Snowflake consumer. That normalization step is what data-dict can provide. > > ### data-dict > > A Rust CLI plus YAML spec (v0.1.0): tables (name/label/description/details, `source`, > columns, constraints), columns (type system with `number(id|ordinal|quantity)`, `units`, > `values`/`range`/`examples`, `display: restricted`, assertions in a constrained SQL-like > sublanguage), `relationships` (`join` expression + `cardinality` + `conflicts`), > `glossary`, and data `version`. Three validation levels: spec, metadata, data. Embedded > agent skills (`data-dict skill read|write`). `source` is parquet-only today, with SQL > sources explicitly planned. Language-agnostic by construction — a self-contained binary, > per Hadley: "easy to run anywhere." > > `site/semantic-models.md` currently argues *against* the dimension/metric split (intent, > not intrinsic property; data scientists can derive columns themselves). That page is > aimed at data scientists exploring data. The commons/querychat audience is different — a > domain expert behind an agent, who cannot derive columns and for whom pre-vetted > aggregations are the trust mechanism. Hadley is open to expanding the definition, so the > question is what shape the expansion takes, not whether. > > ## 2. The vendor formats > > ### Snowflake > > Two formats, one clearly go-forward: > > - **Semantic views** (GA, in-database schema-level objects): logical `TABLES` (with > primary/unique keys, synonyms, comments), `RELATIONSHIPS` (equality, ASOF, and range > joins), `FACTS` (row-level expressions, can be `PRIVATE`), `DIMENSIONS`, `METRICS` > (aggregate expressions, `NON ADDITIVE BY`, window functions), plus AI affordances > attached to the object itself: `WITH SYNONYMS (...)` and `COMMENT` on every element, > `AI_VERIFIED_QUERIES`, `AI_SQL_GENERATION`, `AI_QUESTION_CATEGORIZATION`, and > `WITH CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE` on high-cardinality dimensions. Queried via the > `SEMANTIC_VIEW()` table construct (joins and aggregation resolved by the engine — > definitions "cannot be circumvented"). > - **Legacy Cortex Analyst YAML** (`semantic_model.yaml` on a stage): same shape plus > `sample_values` (the generator wants ~25 per dimension) and `default_aggregation`. > Snowflake has removed its spec page; migration functions exist in both directions. > > The key extraction fact: **`SYSTEM$READ_YAML_FROM_SEMANTIC_VIEW('db.schema.view')` > returns the entire definition as YAML in one SQL call**, in a documented spec > (tables/base_table, dimensions, time_dimensions, facts, metrics, relationships with > `relationship_columns`, verified_queries, custom instructions). This is the ideal > converter input — no DDL parsing, works over any driver. Discovery via > `SHOW SEMANTIC VIEWS` / information_schema. > > Also notable: Cortex Analyst's REST API accepts an *inline* semantic model > (`semantic_model` as a YAML string), so a tool could synthesize a Snowflake semantic > model from a data-dict.yaml on the fly without creating any object in the account. > > ### Databricks > > Two artifacts, converging on one semantic store: > > - **Unity Catalog metric views** (`CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML`): YAML > with `version` (1.1), `source` (table or SQL), `filter`, `joins` (with `cardinality`, > nesting), `fields`/`dimensions` and `measures`, each carrying `name`, `expr`, > `comment`, `display_name`, `synonyms`, `format` — collectively called "agent metadata" > in the docs. Measures support `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, windows, semi-additivity, and > composition via `MEASURE(other_measure)`. Queried with > `SELECT dim, MEASURE(m) ... GROUP BY ALL`. Parameterized views are invoked like table > functions. Extraction: `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED ... AS JSON` returns the complete > YAML in the `View Text` field. > - **Genie** (now "Genie Agents"; API paths still say `spaces`): a curated NL-to-SQL > agent over ≤30 UC tables/views/metric views. Its knowledge store holds text > instructions (docs: "use text instructions only as a last resort"), example SQL > queries, structured SQL expressions in three categories — **measures, filters, > fields/dimensions**, each with `display_name`, `sql`, `synonyms`, usage guidance — > explicit join relationships (PK/FK constraints auto-imported), per-column synonym and > description overrides, entity-matching value dictionaries, and benchmarks. Trusted > assets (parameterized example queries; `RETURNS TABLE` SQL UDFs routed by their > `COMMENT`s) produce answers labeled "Trusted" — the same governed-path/fallback-path > trust split commons implements with tags A/B, and Genie's trusted-asset UDFs are > almost exactly commons `measure()`s expressed as SQL functions. > - The full Genie curation is readable via > `GET /api/2.0/genie/spaces/{id}?include_serialized_space=true`; the `serialized_space` > JSON is complete but **undocumented/unversioned** (export–modify–reimport is the > supported pattern). Genie also has an "Export to Metric View" operation, i.e. > Databricks itself treats metric views as the durable normalized form of Genie > curation. > - Base dictionary harvest: UC table/column comments, PK/FK constraints, via REST > (`/api/2.1/unity-catalog/tables/{full_name}`) or `information_schema`. > - The Genie Conversation API (start-conversation / messages / query-result) lets > external apps ask questions and retrieve generated SQL + results; relevant as a > possible commons *delegation* target, not as a definition source. > > ### Apache Ossie (Open Semantic Interchange) > > Announced Sept 2025 (Snowflake, dbt Labs, Salesforce/Tableau, +), v0.1 spec Jan 2026, > now incubating at Apache as "Ossie" with 60+ orgs including Databricks. Shape: > `semantic_model` with `datasets` (source, primary_key, `fields` with `expression`, > `dimension`, `label`), `relationships`, `metrics`, and `ai_context` + > `custom_extensions` at every level; expressions carry a `dialects` array of > `{dialect, expression}` pairs. Reference converters exist for dbt, GoodData, > Polaris/Snowflake, Salesforce (none for Databricks metric views yet). Young (in-repo > version 0.2.0-dev) and clearly the industry's chosen neutral hub. Don't build on it > yet; do keep data-dict's new field names compatible with its vocabulary > (`expression`/`expr`, `label`, `synonyms`, `ai_context`-like prose fields), and > consider a data-dict ↔ Ossie converter later as the single hop to everything else. > > ## 3. The convergent core > > Field-by-field correspondence (blank = absent): > > | concept | Snowflake sem. view | Databricks metric view | Genie knowledge store | Ossie | data-dict.yaml today | commons today | > |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| > | physical binding | `base_table` | `source` (table/SQL) | UC tables list | `dataset.source` | `source` (parquet only) | `data_source()` | > | table docs | `COMMENT`, synonyms | `comment` | description overrides | `description`, `ai_context` | `label`/`description`/`details` | dictionary first-touch | > | column/dimension | `DIMENSIONS` (`expr`, `data_type`) | `fields` (`expr`) | fields/dimensions snippets | `fields` | `columns` (physical only, typed) | dictionary columns | > | synonyms | `WITH SYNONYMS` | `synonyms` | column synonyms | via `ai_context` | — | — | > | sample values | `sample_values` (legacy), `is_enum` | — | value dictionaries (≤1,024) | — | `values` / `examples` / `range` | rendered from dictionary | > | measure/metric | `METRICS` (agg `expr`, non-additive) | `measures` (agg `expr`, windows) | measure snippets | `metrics` | — | `measure()` (R fn) | > | named filter/segment | `LABELS = (FILTER)`, legacy `filters` | view-level `filter` | filter snippets | — | — | — | > | relationships | `RELATIONSHIPS` (keys; ASOF/range) | `joins` (`on`, `cardinality`) | join relationships (PK/FK auto) | `relationships` | `relationships` (`join` + `cardinality` + `conflicts`) | rendered from dictionary | > | verified queries | `AI_VERIFIED_QUERIES` | — | example/parameterized queries, UDF trusted assets | — | — | (closest: `measure()`) | > | freeform instructions | `AI_SQL_GENERATION`, ... | — | text instructions | `ai_context` | `details`, `glossary` | context layer / system prompt | > | constraints on data | PK/unique on logical tables | — | — | `primary_key` | `constraints` + assertions, validated | — | > | units / PII / time zones | — | `format` (partial) | — | — | `units`, `display: restricted`, `time_zone` | rendered from dictionary | > | glossary | — | — | text instructions | — | `glossary` | system prompt + search | > > Two readings of this table: > > - data-dict's descriptive half is already the strongest column: nothing else validates > against data, types values as carefully, or has `units`/`display: restricted`. The > vendors' `sample_values`/value-dictionary machinery is data-dict's > `values`/`examples` under another name. > - The four rows data-dict is missing — synonyms, metrics, filters, verified queries — > are precisely the rows every vendor agrees on, and precisely what an agent needs for > a governed answer path. > > ## 4. data-dict.yaml as the first-class home of the semantic layer > > The proposal: rather than commons defining its own semantic-layer serialization and > *also* converting vendor formats, data-dict.yaml grows the four missing rows, becoming > the neutral, validated, language-agnostic form. commons (R), querychat (R + Python), > canvas, and anything else then adopt semantic definitions right out of the dictionary, > and vendor conversion becomes "harvest into data-dict" once, rather than N×M adapters. > > ### Sketch > > ```yaml > $version: 0.2.0 > name: sales > tables: > - name: orders > description: One row per completed order since 2020. > source: > sql: sales.orders # already planned for the spec > columns: > - name: order_total > type: number(quantity) > units: USD > range: [0, .inf] > - name: region > type: enum > values: [AMER, EMEA, APAC] > synonyms: [territory, geo] # NEW: per-column synonyms > - name: status_cd > type: enum > values: {90: realized, 10: pending, 20: cancelled} > metrics: # NEW: governed aggregations > - name: net_revenue > label: Net revenue > description: Realized revenue net of discounts. Only status 90 counts. > expr: SUM(order_total * adj_fctr) FILTER (WHERE status_cd = 90) > synonyms: [revenue, sales] > origin: # optional pointer to the system of record > snowflake_semantic_view: SALES_DB.PUBLIC.SALES_METRICS > metric: NET_REVENUE > > filters: # NEW: named segments > - name: enterprise > description: Mid-Market-3 through Enterprise-3 accounts. > expr: tile_size IN ('Mid-Market-3', 'Enterprise-1', 'Enterprise-2', 'Enterprise-3') > synonyms: [MM3 to E3] > > queries: # NEW: verified, parameterized queries > - name: open_opps_in_region > description: Open opportunities in the given regions. > parameters: > - name: regions > type: enum > values: [AMER, EMEA, APAC] > sql: | > SELECT * FROM opportunities > WHERE status = 'open' AND region IN ({regions}) > verified_by: jane > verified_at: 2026-07-01 > ``` > > Design notes: > > - **Two governed shapes are needed, and they're complementary.** Declarative `metrics` > (aggregate `expr` over a table, groupable by any documented column, joins supplied by > the existing `relationships`) are the vendor-convergent shape — this is what imports > from Snowflake metrics and Databricks measures, and what could export back out. > `queries` (full parameterized SQL) are the Genie-trusted-asset / commons-`measure()` > shape — trivially executable, no compiler needed, the right form for vetted logic > that doesn't fit "one aggregate over one grain." Both are governed; both should > exist. (Snowflake's verified queries and Genie's parameterized examples show every > vendor ended up needing the second shape too.) > - **Parameter typing falls out of the existing spec.** A `parameters` entry is just a > column descriptor — `type`, `values`, `range`, `description` — reusing the grammar > data-dict already defines. commons already maps this exact vocabulary onto ellmer > types in `read-measures.R` (`enum[...]`, `number`, `boolean`, ...); a dictionary > parameter converts to a tool argument mechanically. > - **The expression-language question.** data-dict's assertion sublanguage deliberately > excludes aggregates, and extending it to cover metric expressions would mean > building a SQL dialect. Don't: let `expr` be warehouse SQL, as every vendor does. > What the CLI *can* validate cheaply: that referenced columns exist and are > documented, that a metric over a `number(id)` column is flagged (the measures table > in the spec already says ids can't be summed — a genuinely novel check no vendor > performs), and eventually that the compiled query parses/runs against the source. > Dialect portability can follow Ossie's `dialects` array later if needed. > - **`origin` gives the trust story teeth.** A metric harvested from a Snowflake > semantic view keeps a pointer to it; a consumer connected to Snowflake executes via > `SEMANTIC_VIEW()` (engine-enforced, can't drift), and any other consumer compiles > `expr` locally (curated, but client-side). That's the certified vs. curated > distinction from `inst/references/semantic-layer-landscape.md`, encoded in the file. > - **Where the dimension/metric philosophy lands.** The expansion doesn't reclassify > columns: columns stay columns (any of them groupable/filterable — the original > objection to Kimball-style splits holds). Metrics are *additions* — named, > trusted aggregations — not a partition of the columns. `semantic-models.md` would > need updating to reflect the second audience: agents serving people who can't derive > columns themselves. > > ### How commons adopts it > > `data_source(dictionary=)` already parses the dictionary. With metrics/queries > present, commons derives the semantic layer instead of requiring separate authoring: > > ```r > agent <- commons( > ellmer::chat_anthropic(), > data_sources = data_source(con, dictionary = "data-dict.yaml"), > # dictionary metrics and queries become tag-A tools automatically; > # R functions remain for computation SQL can't express > semantic_layer = semantic_layer("R/extra_tools.R") > ) > ``` > > - Each dictionary `query` becomes a governed tool directly: parameters → ellmer types, > SQL template interpolated with safe quoting, executed on the dictionary table's > source. > - Each dictionary `metric` becomes a governed tool with a generated `dimensions` argument > (enum over the table's documented columns) and optional `filters` argument (enum over > named filters); commons compiles > `SELECT , AS FROM [JOIN ...] WHERE GROUP BY ` > — or, when `origin` names a vendor object and the connection matches, emits the > vendor's own query form (`SEMANTIC_VIEW(...)` / `MEASURE(...)`). > - `search_measures`, tags A/B, citations, and the first-touch dictionary machinery all > work unchanged; the semantic layer just gains a second authoring surface. > - Synonyms and filters also improve path B: the fallback SQL prompt can resolve "MM3 to > E3" from a `filters` entry instead of prose. > > This also answers Hadley's "mini data explorer" idea: `label`, `description`, typed > `values`, and `display: restricted` are exactly the metadata a generic table-browser > component for multi-dataset commons apps needs, and the same file drives it. > > ## 5. Conversion paths > > The shared work between commons and data-dict is a harvester — plausibly a `data-dict` > CLI subcommand family (Rust, language-agnostic, credentialed via env/profile the way > warehouse CLIs already are), so R and Python consumers get it for free: > > - **Snowflake → data-dict.** `SHOW SEMANTIC VIEWS` to discover; > `SYSTEM$READ_YAML_FROM_SEMANTIC_VIEW()` per view. Mapping: logical tables → > `tables` (base_table → `source: sql`), dimensions/facts with `expr` equal to a bare > column → column docs (+ `synonyms`), computed dimensions/facts → metrics-adjacent > or dropped initially, metrics → `metrics`, `relationship_columns` → `relationships` > (`join`/`cardinality`), verified queries → `queries`, `AI_*` instructions → > `details`. The legacy stage YAML differs only slightly (`sample_values` → > `examples`, `default_aggregation`, `relationship_type` → `cardinality`). > - **Databricks → data-dict.** Three layers, all machine-readable: > `information_schema`/UC REST (comments, PK/FK → columns, constraints, > relationships); metric views via `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED ... AS JSON` (fields → > columns, measures → `metrics`, joins → `relationships`, synonyms/display_name → > `synonyms`/`label`); Genie `serialized_space` via one GET (SQL snippets → `metrics` > and `filters`, example/parameterized queries and table-function trusted assets → > `queries`, value dictionaries → `values`). The Genie JSON is undocumented, so treat > that leg as best-effort behind the stable two. > - **data-dict → vendor** (later, lower priority): generate `CREATE SEMANTIC VIEW` DDL > or metric-view YAML, or feed Cortex Analyst's inline `semantic_model` parameter > directly. Valuable for orgs that want to author once in data-dict and light up > Genie/Cortex. > - **Ossie**: revisit once the spec stabilizes; a single data-dict ↔ Ossie converter > would then subsume much of the above. No Databricks metric-view converter exists in > their repo yet — contributing one is an option if Posit wants a seat in that > conversation. > > ## 6. What querychat and other downstream tools inherit > > - querychat already reads data-dict.yaml; with metrics/filters/queries in the file it > can render them as governed SQL snippets in its prompt (its Genie-style "prefer these > exact expressions" pattern) instead of, or in addition to, inlining raw Snowflake > DDL. Its existing semantic-view discovery becomes "harvest to data-dict, then render" > — one rendering path for all sources, in both R and Python. > - canvas (and any other agentic consumer) gets the same: one file to read for tables, > meaning, trusted metrics, and vetted queries, regardless of warehouse. > - The trust gradient travels with the file: engine-enforced (`origin` + live vendor > connection) > compiled dictionary metric/query (curated, validated by CLI) > > documented column (descriptive) > free prose (context). Each consumer can surface > its own version of commons' A/B tags from the same metadata. > > ## 7. Risks and open questions > > - **Scope creep for data-dict.** The expansion adds executable semantics to a > documentation format; validation levels keep the line clear (spec-validating a > metric ≠ certifying it), but the spec's identity ("what the raw data means") shifts. > This is the conversation to have with Hadley — his write-up invitation suggests he's > already partway there. > - **SQL dialect in `expr`/`sql`.** Unavoidable (all vendors accept it); mitigations are > the `origin` pointer, CLI parse checks per known dialect, and Ossie's dialect-array > pattern if portability becomes real demand. > - **Compilation correctness in commons.** Compiling metric queries client-side means > commons owns join-path selection (fan-out/double-counting hazards the engines handle > natively). Start with single-table metrics + explicit dictionary relationships; > prefer `origin` execution when available. > - **Genie's `serialized_space` is unstable.** Fine for a best-effort harvester; not a > foundation. > - **Multi-user/lifetime issues** (issue #29, #25) are orthogonal but interact with > metric/query execution if compiled queries run on shared connections. > - **Naming: settled.** The spec uses the vendor-conventional terms — `metrics` for > declarative aggregates (Snowflake METRICS, dbt metrics, Ossie `metrics`), `queries` > for verified parameterized SQL. commons is pre-release and renames its vocabulary to > match (`measure()` and "measure" throughout; note `measure()` today is really the > `queries` shape, an executable with typed parameters). One collision to avoid: > data-dict already uses "measure" for the `number(id|ordinal|quantity)` qualifier, > another reason not to introduce a second meaning of the word there. > > ## 8. Suggested next steps > > - [ ] Share this report's section 4 sketch with Hadley as a concrete proposal for the > data-dict expansion (metrics, filters, queries, synonyms; parameter descriptors > reusing the column grammar). > - [ ] Prototype in commons without waiting on the spec: accept `metrics`/`queries` > keys in `data_dictionary()` behind the existing normalization, derive tag-A > tools from them, and validate against a hand-written dictionary for a demo > source. Rename commons' "measure" vocabulary to match along the way. > - [ ] Prototype the Snowflake leg: `SYSTEM$READ_YAML_FROM_SEMANTIC_VIEW` → data-dict > converter (could start as an R script in commons; graduate to the data-dict CLI). > - [ ] Prototype the Databricks leg: information_schema + `DESCRIBE ... AS JSON` → > data-dict; treat Genie serialized_space as a stretch goal. > - [ ] Coordinate with querychat on rendering dictionary metrics/queries in its > prompt, replacing raw-DDL inlining as the normalized path. > - [ ] Track Apache Ossie; revisit a data-dict ↔ Ossie converter when their spec cuts a > stable release. > > ## File references > > - commons: `R/data-dictionary.R`, `R/measures.R`, `R/read-measures.R`, `R/tools.R`, > `R/data-source.R`, `inst/references/semantic-layer-landscape.md`, > `inst/references/context-semantic-graph-layers.md`, issue posit-dev/commons#6 > - data-dict (`~/Documents/rrr/data-dict`): `site/spec.md`, `site/semantic-models.md`, > `README.md` > - querychat (`~/Documents/rrr/querychat`): `pkg-r/R/DataDict.R`, `pkg-r/R/DBISource.R` > (lines ~496–646), `pkg-r/inst/prompts/semantic-views/`, > `pkg-py/src/querychat/_snowflake.py` > - Snowflake: [semantic views overview](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/views-semantic/overview), > [YAML spec](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/views-semantic/semantic-view-yaml-spec), > [SYSTEM$READ_YAML_FROM_SEMANTIC_VIEW](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/system_read_yaml_from_semantic_view), > [views vs. legacy models](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/views-semantic/semantic-models-vs-views), > [Cortex Analyst REST API](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-analyst/rest-api) > - Databricks: [metric views YAML reference](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/metric-views/yaml-ref), > [Genie overview](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/), > [Genie best practices](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/best-practices), > [trusted assets](https://docs.databricks.com/en/genie/trusted-assets.html), > [Genie REST API](https://docs.databricks.com/api/workspace/genie), > [Conversation API](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/conversation-api), > [UC Tables API](https://docs.databricks.com/api/workspace/tables/get) > - Ossie/OSI: [site](https://open-semantic-interchange.org/), > [spec repo](https://github.com/open-semantic-interchange/OSI), > [Apache incubation](https://ossie.apache.org/updates/ossie-enters-apache-incubator/)

title: Broaden semantic layer definition
description: Currently just a set of measures. The usual usage of this term is broader; some of the information that we're currently recommending to push to the context layer should live in the semantic layer itself.

title: be sure to tell the agent that the user can see plots
description:
Can't remember if I made this clear in the prompting introduced yesterday.

Also related to #56—should be the case for the output types that are made visible broadly.

title: Consider exporting trajectory reviews as markdown
description:
`trajectory_review()` currently adds flags and notes to an append-only JSONL event log. 

Consider instead exporting them as agent-friendly markdown, complete with the conversation and all notes and flags. Maybe similar to what plannotator does. 

See https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/80#discussion_r3715195276

title: Including measure outputs in the chat
description:
It's preferable that tables are shown in the chat deterministically rather than the LLM repeating them. What if the agent could write e.g. `r r3` inline in the assistant text and it would be rendered there? 

Related to #56.

title: Plot / other rich output types for measures
description: Right now, you _can_ output e.g. a plot from a measure but it doesn't get shown in the UI.

description:
`run_sql` is described as “read-only” in the tool schema, its MCP-style annotation, and the package documentation, but the current implementation does not enforce that property.

[`source_query()` calls `check_query()` and then passes the original string to `DBI::dbGetQuery()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/a9b1ee23f41c9f757a4eb079f9d0cf512c43a130/R/data-source.R#L455-L480). [`check_query()` only rejects a denylisted keyword at the start of the string](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/a9b1ee23f41c9f757a4eb079f9d0cf512c43a130/R/data-source.R#L482-L519). It neither requires a `SELECT` nor requires exactly one statement.

## Reproducer on current `main`

```r
pkgload::load_all(".")

src <- data_source(sales = data.frame(x = 1L))
sql <- "SELECT 1 AS ok; DROP TABLE sales;"

check_query(sql)       # accepted
source_query(src, sql) # executes the DROP (with a DBI warning)
DBI::dbExistsTable(src$con, "sales")
#> [1] FALSE
```

I reproduced this with R 4.6.0 and DuckDB 1.5.5. The owned DuckDB configuration lock does not prevent local DDL/DML. Other non-`SELECT` statement classes such as `SET` and `PRAGMA` also pass `check_query()`; their effects depend on the supplied connection and its privileges.

Consequently, these currently overstate the guarantee:

- [`read_only_hint = TRUE`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/blob/a9b1ee23f41c9f757a4eb079f9d0cf512c43a130/R/tools.R#L234-L244)
- “Run a read-only SELECT query”
- “The `run_sql` tool runs only read-only `SELECT` queries”

## Proposal: classify DuckDB SQL with DuckDB's parser

For DuckDB-backed sources, use core `json_serialize_sql()` before executing agent-authored SQL:

1. Quote the candidate with `DBI::dbQuoteString()` and pass it as the required constant string. `json_serialize_sql()` parses; it does not execute the candidate.
2. Reject missing output, parser/serializer errors, and `error: true`.
3. Require exactly one serialized statement.
4. Require the root node to be `SELECT_NODE`.
5. Recursively inspect function nodes and reject dynamic-SQL executors such as `query()` / `query_table()` rather than trusting their string arguments.
6. Add known-good/known-bad canaries and fail closed if DuckDB changes the JSON shape.

This handles the immediate cases structurally:

- `SELECT 1; SELECT 2` serializes as two statements.
- `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE sales` returns `error: true` because the serializer only admits `SELECT` statements.
- quoted or qualified function spellings normalize to the same AST `function_name`.

We use this DuckDB AST-serialization pattern in pi-bio-agent to detect normalized dynamic-SQL calls ([implementation](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/pi-bio-agent/blob/73f1b28c36c7288ae2d000236ac138983f02bd44/src/core/sql-guard.ts#L215-L230)) and to inspect function calls without SQL-text matching ([implementation and fail-closed behavior](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/pi-bio-agent/blob/73f1b28c36c7288ae2d000236ac138983f02bd44/src/duckdb/plan-hermeticity.ts#L87-L121)). It also has a parser/plan format canary so version drift disables the claimed property rather than silently weakening it ([canary](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/pi-bio-agent/blob/73f1b28c36c7288ae2d000236ac138983f02bd44/src/duckdb/plan-hermeticity.ts#L124-L145)).

`data_source()` also accepts arbitrary DBI connections and SQL dialects, so DuckDB's parser cannot prove those statements read-only. That path needs a backend-specific validator and/or a genuinely read-only connection. Until it has one, I suggest describing the weaker guarantee accurately and setting `read_only_hint = FALSE` for sources where commons cannot enforce it.

## Suggested regression coverage

- Reject the stacked-statement reproducer and verify `sales` still exists.
- Reject a second `SELECT`, DDL/DML, `SET`, and `PRAGMA`.
- Accept one `SELECT` / `WITH ... SELECT`.
- Do not reject keywords or semicolons inside literals, quoted identifiers, or comments.
- Reject quoted and qualified dynamic-SQL function calls.
- Fail closed when AST serialization is unavailable or its expected JSON shape changes.

---

_Disclosure: This issue was generated in Pi using GPT Sol 5.6 High._

title: Inline citation attachment can break block Markdown and hide verified citations
description:
## Problem

PR #107 originally preserved the whitespace before each verified citation aside.

Commit `f0a46de` added logic that removes this whitespace. The scanner now places
the aside directly after the preceding visible text.

This behavior can break Markdown blocks. A verified citation can disappear from
the user interface, while Commons still records the answer as `Cited`.

## Regression

The last PR commit before the later changes was `5b497232`. For an answer that
ends with a fenced code block, that version produced this structure:

````markdown
```r
1 + 1
```

<shiny-aside ...>
````

After `f0a46de`, the scanner produces this structure:

````markdown
```r
1 + 1
```<shiny-aside ...>
````

The `<shiny-aside>` text becomes part of the code block because the closing
fence is no longer valid Markdown.

The merged state of PR #107, at `426236d`, contains this behavior.

## User impact

I reproduced these results in a real shinychat browser:

- A plain paragraph showed one citation pill.
- A fenced code block showed no citation pill. The aside markup appeared inside
  the code block.
- A Markdown table showed no citation pill. The citation quote appeared as a
  separate blockquote.

The server still records the citation decision as accepted. `stream_async()`
therefore derives provenance tag `B`.

Tag `B` does not get a separate provenance aside. Its citation is expected to
provide the visible trust indicator. The user can therefore see no citation
indicator, while the trace records the answer as `Cited`.

This breaks the contract in PR #107. The displayed provenance and the recorded
provenance no longer represent the same result.

## Root cause

`R/citation-scan.R` now keeps trailing whitespace in
`pending_whitespace`. `emit_attachment()` removes that whitespace when prior
visible text exists:

```r
if (has_attachment_target) {
  pending_whitespace <<- ""
}
```

The scanner does not determine whether the preceding text ends with block
Markdown. It always joins the aside to that text.

## Test gap

The scanner test added with `f0a46de` uses a plain sentence. It asserts that the
aside immediately follows the sentence.

The browser fixture also uses paragraph content. It does not cover answers that
end with:

- A fenced code block
- A Markdown table
- Other block Markdown that requires a line boundary

## Expected behavior

Citation projection must preserve the structure of preceding Markdown blocks.
A verified citation must remain visible when it causes provenance tag `B`.

Add browser regression tests for fenced code blocks and tables. These tests
must also make sure that an accepted citation produces visible citation UI.

title: citation markers might not increment
description:
Looking at this a bit more closely, I think this change also introduces some correctness issues, due to how de-duplicating works in `<shiny-aside>` that have the same labels. Here is a relevant excerpt from Claude:

```
### Numbered markers don't survive more than one citation

This is the one I'd push back on hardest, because the new prompt makes it the common case. shinychat merges adjacent asides that carry a non-empty label into a single shiny-aside-group (jI()/kS() in shinychat.js). I confirmed in a real browser with two attached citation asides:

2 asides, different sources → 1 pill:
  aria-label: "documentation (+1 more)"
  ::before:   counter(commons-citation)     → renders "1"
  .shiny-aside-pill__overflow: display:block, text "+1"

2 asides, same source → 1 pill, visible text just "1"

So:
- The counter never reaches 2. "Restore numbered citation markers" yields a constant 1.
- The second source's name never appears on the pill face at all.
- When sources differ, the marker visually reads "1+1" — the CSS hides img and .shiny-aside-pill__label but not .shiny-aside-pill__overflow, which computes to display: block inside an inline-flex superscript.

The existing browser tests don't catch this: the fixture has exactly one verified citation, and the new R-level test ("adjacent verified citations attach to the preceding text") asserts on the R output string only, never on the rendered DOM.

There's a cleaner path available: shinychat has native footnote numbering for asides without a label (shiny-aside-pill--count, aria-label: "Aside N", index assigned by Dj()), and unlabeled asides are not merged — each gets its own group. That gets real per-citation numbering for free. The trade-off is the accessible name becomes "Aside 1" instead of "documentation"; the source name would live in the popover only.
```

_Originally posted by @cpsievert in https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/107#discussion_r3798637808_

title: fallback for `run_r` sandbox on older Linux kernel versions
description:
It seems like some small subset (Fable later guessed 10-15%) of deployments will not have a new-enough Linux kernel to use Landlock. "5.13+ with Landlock enabled, which in terms of Connect's supported OSes means Ubuntu 22.04+, RHEL 9.6+, or RHEL 10 — and rules out RHEL 8 entirely." We'll need to decide whether to support an unsandboxed `run_r` fallback. Maybe just error by default and allow users to set some argument, option or envvar to disable the sandbox?
Write-up from Fable

Here's the picture. Short version: **Connect's version doesn't matter — nothing in Connect gates or blocks the sandbox. The constraint is entirely the kernel: 5.13+ with Landlock enabled, which in terms of Connect's supported OSes means Ubuntu 22.04+, RHEL 9.6+, or RHEL 10 — and rules out RHEL 8 entirely.** **What the commons sandbox needs from the kernel.** `src/sandbox.c` uses three mechanisms, and only one is demanding: - Landlock, via raw `landlock_create_ruleset`/`add_rule`/`restrict_self` syscalls, using only the 13 ABI-v1 filesystem rights (`FS_V1_ALL`). That's the floor introduced in kernel 5.13, so any Landlock-enabled kernel suffices — but Landlock must be compiled in *and* active in the boot LSM list, not just "kernel ≥ 5.13". - seccomp filter mode via `prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP, ...)` plus `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` — both kernel 3.5+, a non-issue on anything Connect runs. - `setrlimit(RLIMIT_AS)` — ancient. Note the failure mode is hard, not graceful: on Linux, `worker_init()` always engages the sandbox and `c_sandbox_engage` raises if `landlock_create_ruleset` fails, so on a kernel without Landlock, `run_r` doesn't degrade to unsandboxed — it errors. **What Connect contributes.** I pulled and searched `posit-dev/connect` (it was cloned at `~/Documents/rrr/connect`): every seccomp/Landlock reference in the tree is in vendored k8s/golang.org libraries. Connect's own content launching goes through `rsandbox` (`job/sandbox/sandbox.go` → `ext/rsandbox`), which is a setuid helper doing run-as-user, mount/user namespaces, and rlimits — it installs no seccomp filter and doesn't set `no_new_privs`, so it can't block the syscalls the worker needs. The Kubernetes launcher (`kubernetes/resource_bases.go`) sets only `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup`/`supplementalGroups` in the pod security context, no `seccompProfile`. So there's no minimum Connect version; any release runs this fine given a suitable kernel. **Mapping to Connect's supported OSes** (`docs/admin/getting-started/requirements/index.md`): | OS | Kernel | Landlock | | ---------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 / 26.04 | 5.15 / 6.8+ | Enabled by default since 22.04 GA (ABI 1 on 22.04, ABI 4+ on 24.04) | | RHEL 10 | 6.12 | Enabled | | RHEL 9 | 5.14 | Only from **RHEL 9.6** (`kernel-5.14.0-568.el9`), where Red Hat enabled it by default and backported up to ABI 5 | | RHEL 8 | 4.18 | Never — `run_r` will hard-fail here | | SLES 15 SP6/SP7 | 6.4 | Kernel is new enough, but I couldn't confirm it's in SUSE's default LSM list — worth a `dmesg \| grep landlock` check | For off-host/container execution, the kernel is the K8s node's, and since Connect doesn't set a `seccompProfile`, pods run seccomp-unconfined unless cluster policy forces `RuntimeDefault` — and even then, current containerd/Docker default profiles allowlist the landlock syscalls. Consistent with what we saw earlier on connect.posit.it (Landlock ABI 7, everything working). So the one deployment population that genuinely can't use this is RHEL 8 hosts and RHEL 9 ≤ 9.5 hosts under native execution. If that matters, options are a capability check up front (`sandbox_capabilities()` already surfaces the ABI) with a clearer error, or an explicit opt-out — but as written, the "sandbox must engage" stance means those hosts just can't run `run_r`. Sources: [Is Landlock LSM available in RHEL? (Red Hat)](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7028727), [Ubuntu bug #1953192 "Enable Landlock by default"](https://bugs.launchpad.net/bugs/1953192), [landlock(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/landlock.7.html), [containerd default seccomp profile](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/main/contrib/seccomp/seccomp_default.go)
